This lecture carries content rather than logistics, and the orientation deck holds the mechanics of the semester. The lecture leaves you with four maps and one posture. The four maps are the seven-layer stack, the five-stage progression to agentic AI, the definition of an agent from PEAS to the nine components, and the framework board with every box assigned to an Evolution. The posture is that the human is index zero, and the Degradation Pattern describes what happens when the human stops being index zero. Four words describe the semester (survey, build, govern, defend), and this Evolution covers the survey and govern pair. [0:00–0:02]

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development / Dr. Jeffry Babb · Paul and Virginia Engler College of Business · West Texas A&M University

The lecture has five parts. The first part frames the course. The second part reads two maps. The third part defines an agent and works one example on a slide, a chat assistant against Claude Code. The fourth part makes the case for governance. The fifth part presents the instrument you will use in every Evolution and the Evolution 0 brief.

Cut from slide 2 (full wording):
- Layers of AI (and the one everybody forgets); AI & ML → Agentic AI; the framework board, every box assigned to a week
- Russell & Norvig and PEAS; the LLM agent loop and its halt; the nine components; a worked Design Analysis: chat assistant vs. Claude Code

The course asks two questions. The survey question asks why: what problem each design answered and what the design cost, rather than what is fashionable this month. The build question asks whether you can make such a system and answer for it. Tree Hollow is your first reading because it states the stake: a system can produce an answer without being able to answer for it. Ask the class who answered for the last piece of generated code they shipped, and wait for answers. The definition that runs the semester follows from that question. A language model is a reasoner with no persistent state, no ground truth, and no accountability. Every component this course studies is an attempt to supply one of those three things from outside the model. Governance supplies the third, and no software can automate it, because accountability belongs to a person. [~7 min]

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- Why was each system built that way, what problem did it answer, and what did it cost? Historical order, one component model.
- Answerability / A model has no persistent state, no ground truth, and no accountability. Everything stacked on top of it (tools, memory, evaluators, governance) exists to supply those three. The engineer's role, which no component can take over, is to answer for the system. The course structure (flight cards, consultations, attestations) has you perform that role each week, with evidence.

The first map has seven layers, and you can read it top down or bottom up. Agentic AI sits on top with memory, planning, tool use, and autonomous execution. Under it sit generative AI, deep learning, neural networks, machine learning, and classical AI, and at the bottom sits the data foundation: ownership, definitions, quality, lineage. The figure draws the layers as a widening stack because every agentic system stands on all of them. Nothing at the top replaces anything below. Classical planning did not die; it returned as 'planning' in LLM agents. For this reason a Design Analysis starts at the bottom, with the question of what the system stands on. [~5 min]

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- How to read it / Agentic AI is the newest and thinnest layer. The data foundation is the oldest, and it has cracks. / Every Design Analysis starts at the bottom: what model, what weights, what data does this thing stand on, and is it local or hosted? / Two passes on any system: what does it claim (top-down) and what does it stand on (bottom-up). / The foundation shows through in E7 (memory on embeddings) and E11 (what your evaluation data actually is).

The data foundation is easy to forget because it is unglamorous and because its cost lands later, on someone else. The framework image lists four words for it: ownership, definitions, quality, lineage. Each one returns as a failure later in the semester. Ownership asks on whose behalf the agent may act. Definitions matter because the agent inherits every ambiguity in your schema, and 'done' is the most dangerous word in the course: an agent with no definition of done reports it on its own terms. For this reason the course gives done a closed vocabulary (Completed, Completed — Partial, Dropped), and a human attests it only after reading the evidence. Quality matters because retrieval returns what is stored: in Evolution 7 you will poison your own memory store with one false fact and watch it propagate. Lineage matters because without provenance a polished summary becomes a fact, which is the ten-deep summary-laundering chain you read in Evolution 9. The Sprint and Drift essay 'Newtonian motion' argues that the cost of generated code is deferred, never erased. [~2 min]

Cut from slide 5 (full wording):
- The Newtonian-motion argument (Sprint and Drift, E9) holds that generated code defers its cost and does not erase it. The foundation is where the deferred cost comes due.

The second map runs five stages left to right, and the unit of work changes at each stage. AI and ML turns data into a decision. Deep learning stacks networks for harder decisions. Generative AI produces an artifact: text, code, an image. AI agents take on a task: they call tools, plan, remember, and keep a human in the loop. Agentic AI automates a process: many agents, protocols between them, delegation, intent preserved across handoffs, rollback, evaluators, cost management, observability, governance. The small text in the last two columns is the syllabus, and the course lives there. Evolutions 1 through 7 build the AI Agents column on your system, and Evolutions 8 through 12 build the Agentic AI column. [~4 min]

- tool use & function calling · planning (ReAct, CoT, ToT) · goal decomposition · memory systems · context management · human-in-the-loop · self-reflection & error recovery
- multi-agent collaboration · agent protocols · delegation & handoff · intent preservation · rollback · feedback loops & evaluators · cost & resource mgmt · observability · governance & guardrails
- The course lives in the last two stages. E1–E7 build the AI Agents column on your system; E8–E12 build the Agentic AI column. Note what changes at each step: the unit of work goes from a decision, to an artifact, to a task, to a process.

The road map shows the same five stages as stops. You consume stops one through three rather than build them: the models, the networks, and the generative capability come from a vendor or an open-weight release. You build stops four and five in this course: an agent that takes on a task, then an agentic system that automates a process. Keep this picture, because each Evolution states which stop it is at. [~1 min]

The framework board can also be read as rings out from the foundation: foundation, creation, core systems, action, full automation. Rings state how far a system's capability extends outward. The columns on the previous slide state when each capability arrived in the field's history. Hold both readings. A system that claims ring five and runs on ring two is a generative model with a loop bolted on, with no memory, no evaluator, and no governance, and vendors sell such systems as agentic. By the end of this lecture you will be able to say why that gap matters. The exercise for Evolution 0 is to mark every box on the board for which you can cite a concrete system, and the blanks become your reading list for the semester. [~3 min]

This table gives the fill-in order. I have placed every box on the framework board in one of the twelve Evolutions. Two features of the table need attention. First, the middle is inverted from the catalog order: tools and MCP come before context and memory. Since 2024, tool results have filled most of an agent harness's context window, so the course teaches tools before context management, and MCP is a tool protocol that requires function calling understood first. Second, the two starred Evolutions run on a local open-weight model no matter which route you chose, because tool calling with a small model is brittle, and the brittleness shows you the mechanism, and because embeddings are cheap locally. You do not need to memorize the table. You need to know it exists so that in every Evolution you can say where you are on the board. [~3 min]

Before the definition of an agent, the reasoner in the middle of it needs a precise statement. A language model adds a reasoner that generalizes from text. Classical agents never had that reasoner, and its arrival is why the agent loops of 2023 appeared. The model lacks three things: persistent state, ground truth, and accountability. Those three things organize the semester. Context and memory supply state. Tools, retrieval, and evaluators supply ground truth. Governance supplies accountability, and more software cannot supply it, because accountability is a property of a person. [~2 min]

Cut from slide 10 (full wording):
- A reasoner that generalizes from text. /  / It can read an unfamiliar error, propose a plan, write the call, and explain itself in prose. This capability made the 2023 wave of LLM agents possible, and the classical agents of chapter 4 never had it.
- It cannot answer for anything. Governance and the human interface (E0, E5, E9, E11) supply answerability, and no automation can supply it in their place.

The definition of an agent predates the language model and still holds. Russell and Norvig define an agent as anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators, and the agent function maps percept sequences to actions. You specify an agent by PEAS: performance measure, environment, actuators, sensors. The performance measure deserves attention, because the 2023 loops never wrote one down, and for this reason they ran until the budget was gone. The five agent types form a ladder: reflex, model-based, goal-based, utility-based, learning. BDI and FIPA supply the multi-agent vocabulary, so when you meet CrewAI in Evolution 8 you will recognize a 1990s design with a language model in the reasoner slot. Your first exercise in Evolution 0 is to specify your intended system by PEAS. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 11 (full wording):
- Agent types, in increasing sophistication: simple reflex · model-based · goal-based · utility-based · learning. BDI (belief–desire–intention) and FIPA multi-agent platforms are the pre-LLM coordination vocabulary; the course returns to them in E8.

The LLM agent loop puts a language model in the reasoner slot. The loop perceives the prompt, tool results, files, and events. It reasons with one model call that emits a thought and a decision. It acts with either a tool call or a final answer. Then it asks the question the whole loop turns on: halt? If the answer is no, the observation goes back in as the next percept. ReAct, from Yao and colleagues in 2022, is the canonical form: thought, action, observation, interleaved. Every later Evolution adds tools, memory, coordination, and evaluation to this loop. ReAct lacked memory, a budget, and verification. The halt condition is what 2023 forgot: AutoGPT and BabyAGI were this loop with a goal and nothing to stop it. Sortie 1 is a loop that halts, on every input class, within budget, with every turn in the ledger. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 12 (full wording):
- Thought → Action → Observation, interleaved, until the model emits a final answer. Every later week adds components to this loop. ReAct lacked memory, a budget, and verification.
- AutoGPT and BabyAGI (spring 2023) ran the loop with goals but with no grounding, no budget, and no evaluator. They spiraled. A loop without a halt keeps calling the model, and every call adds to the bill. Sortie 1 is 'a governed loop that halts.'

The nine components are how you take every system apart this semester, and their order matters. The list runs from what the system stands on, to what it sees, to how it thinks, to how it acts, to what it remembers, to how it coordinates, to what checks it, to where the human is, to how it runs. Each component carries a question and, in teal, the failure that appears when the component is missing or weak. The failures preview the incident casebook: injection is a perception failure, a spiral is a planning failure, summary laundering is a coordination failure, and governance theater is a failure of component eight. A Design Analysis consists of nine short answers and one paragraph on why. [~3 min]

The Evolution 0 exercise, done on a slide, compares a chat assistant (left column) with an agent harness such as Claude Code or Codex CLI (right column) across the nine rows. The foundation is the same hosted model. Perception changes: the harness sees the repo, the shell, tool results, and an instruction file. Planning changes: the chat assistant has one turn, and the human is the loop, while the harness runs an open ReAct loop with plan mode and subagents. Tools: the chat assistant has none, and the harness has a built-in set plus MCP with permission prompts and hooks. Memory: both are bound to the window, but the harness compacts and reads an instruction file. Coordination: a single session against a main session plus subagents. Evaluation: in both, the human does most of it. Governance: the chat assistant has a human on every turn by construction, and the harness has a human in the loop per tool call, with attestation implicit. Runtime: a web page against a terminal with background and cloud sessions. The why paragraph follows from the rows. The harness owns the loop so that the vendor can ship tools, hooks, compaction, and subagents as features, and that ownership of the loop is what makes it an agent. The cost is that governance is per call and implicit, and nothing records what was attested. gzkit, the reference design, fills that gap one tier up. The comparison does not rank the chat assistant below the harness: the chat assistant is a workflow with the human as the loop, and a workflow is the right design wherever the path is known in advance. [~4 min]

Cut from slide 14 (full wording):
- The harness owns the loop so the vendor can ship tools, permissions, hooks, compaction, and subagents as product features: that is what turns a generative system into an agent (components 3, 4, 6, 9 appear). /  / The cost: governance is per-call and implicit. Every tool call asks 'allow?', and by week four you are pressing yes without reading. Nothing records what was attested. The reference design, gzkit, fills that gap (component 8) one tier up. /  / The chat assistant is a workflow with the human as the loop. When the path of a task is known, a workflow is the better design.

Two distinctions carry out of this Evolution. The first comes from Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents': a workflow calls the model along code paths you wrote, and an agent lets the model direct its own control flow. Anthropic recommends the workflow wherever the path is known in advance, and the open loop only where it is not, and in Evolution 2 you will write down which one you chose and why. The second distinction is historical. The field carried PEAS, planning, and coordination protocols forward from the pre-LLM era. The loops of 2023 dropped explicit state, halt conditions, and evaluation against an environment, and the field has rediscovered each of them since. Reinforcement learning had already described reward hacking, so gaming the gate has a history older than the language model. [~2 min]

Cut from slide 15 (full wording):
- Workflow: the model is called along predefined code paths; control lives in your code. /  / Agent: the model directs its own control flow: it decides which tool, when, and whether to continue. /  / When the path is known, a workflow is the better design because it is predictable, cheap, and testable. Reach for an open loop only when the path cannot be known in advance. E2 refactors your loop into a standard pattern (chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator–workers, evaluator–optimizer) and makes you write down why.
- Carried forward / PEAS and the agent function / Planning (STRIPS → goal decomposition) / Coordination protocols (FIPA, contract net → A2A, crews) / Dropped in 2023, rediscovered since / Explicit state (→ context engineering, ledgers) / Halt conditions and budgets (→ governed loops) / Evaluation against an environment (→ evals as gates); reward hacking (→ gaming the gate, failure mode 9)

The Degradation Pattern, from gzkit's why.md, is the reason I built the course the way I did. In week one you prompt carefully and read every line. In week two you skim the diff and trust the green checkmarks. In week three you batch approvals, and 'looks good' becomes reflexive. In week four you approve pull requests you did not read for code you do not understand. Nobody decides to lose control; control slips away one 'looks good' at a time. Three related failures travel with it: cognitive surrender, in which you delegate the judgment rather than the task; mediated observation, in which you see the summary and never the artifact; and governance theater, in which every check passes and nobody verified anything. Ask the class where on this curve each of them was last week. The first exercise in chapter three is a one-week log of your own review behavior. [~4 min]

The Zero Doctrine answers the Degradation Pattern: the human is index zero. First in priority, because your intent drives every decision. Final in authority, because you sign off, and the model does not. And the position cannot be automated away, because accountability is a property of a person. The word zero has its own history in the reference design: it began as zero overhead, became zero drift, and settled as index zero. The covenant has five clauses, and both parties are bound. The human defines intent. The agent operates within constraints and flags violations. Verification is mutual. The human attests after observing the artifacts rather than the summary. Artifacts survive sessions. The covenant has two sides: gates constrain the agent, and the human must engage. Gates alone produce theater. The three concerns (specification, methodology, governance) need each other, and the sentence on the slide is the founding argument of the reference design. It comes from a conversation in January in which the model said only specification matters and the operator refused. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 17 (full wording):
- Two sides: gates constrain agents, and humans must engage (read everything, insist on Q&A). Gates without human engagement produce theater. “Specification without governance drifts; governance without methodology is theater; methodology without specification is arbitrary.”

Five gates enforce the covenant. ADR records intent before implementation. TDD derives tests from the spec, with the red witnessed before the green. The Docs gate checks that what is written matches what runs. BDD supplies acceptance scenarios for anything with an external contract. Human means that someone looked at the artifacts and signed. The gates run in two lanes. Lite is gates one and two, and the weekly Evolutions live there. Heavy is all five, and the Final System lives there. There are two lanes rather than one because ceremony must earn its place. Human attestation at the brief level is universal in both lanes, and there is no self-close path. The command doctrine is the source of the flight vocabulary in this course. Degani and Wiener's Four P's run philosophy, policies, procedures, practices. The cockpit is the model because it is the one place where engineers have built authority over an automated system for decades. The doctrine has four rules: accountability is non-transferable; authority must be instrumented, not asserted; the model is a crew resource, not a crew member; evidence is artifacts, not narration. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 18 (full wording):
- Degani & Wiener: philosophy → policies → procedures → practices. The cockpit serves as the model because aviation has engineered human authority over automated systems for decades. /  / • Accountability is non-transferable. / • Authority must be instrumented, not asserted. / • The model is a crew resource, not a crew member. / • Evidence is artifacts, not narration.
- Evolutions run Lite (gates 1–2). The Final System closes out Heavy (1–5). * Every brief requires human attestation. No path lets an agent close its own brief. Closed vocabulary: Completed · Completed — Partial · Dropped.

The posture needs its place among the governance frameworks, so that nobody mistakes it for the whole of AI governance. Policy frameworks (NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001) tell an organization what must be true, and they are silent on what one engineer and one agent do in one session. Frontier-lab safety frameworks and system cards govern the model, and in Evolution 11 you will read one as a Design Analysis. The practitioner literature on auditing describes an accountability gap: audits without access, standards without enforcement, attestations nobody observed. A covenant is one engineer's answer to that gap. It sits below policy, inside the session, at the level of the artifact. It cannot make a model safe, certify an organization, or substitute for law. Its scope is one build, and it makes the engineer who signed answerable for that build. [~2 min]

Cut from slide 19 (full wording):
- Organizational risk management: map, measure, manage, govern. This framework is necessary, and it says nothing about what one engineer and one agent do in one session.
- The industry's evaluation genre: what was tested, what was found. E11 reads one as a Design Analysis. A system card covers the model and leaves your use of the model unaddressed.
- Audits without access, standards without enforcement, attestations nobody observed. The practitioner literature identifies the gap. A covenant is one engineer's answer to it.
- Where it fits: below policy, inside the session, at the level of the artifact. Where it does not: it cannot make a model safe, certify an organization, or substitute for law. Its scope is one build, which it makes answerable through artifacts and attestation.

State the preservation mechanism, which is what keeps the intent alive after the person who decided has left the session. The format on the right is short on purpose: about a hundred and fifty words, nine lines, one paragraph, five items. I will ask you about it in consultation. [~2 min]

CIDM6333_E10_Lecture_EvalsAsGates.pptx:
Evolution 10. In Sortie 9 an adversary from another model family refuted a planted falsehood, and the receipt went in the log. This Evolution turns the same procedure on your own checks: you plant a falsehood in your own suite and ask whether the suite catches it. Evaluation is falsification, and that sentence frames this Evolution. A check that has never failed tells you nothing about the code it covers, because a green record cannot distinguish a check that can fail from one that cannot. The survey covers the agent benchmarks the field has used since 2023, read for what their graders check, and what happened to several of them in 2026. The build is a golden set, a regression delta, and a RED witness, wired to a gate that exits non-zero. The lab is self-guided and small; the full test points fly in the Sprint.

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- Evolution 10 · Lecture
- Golden sets, regression deltas, judges and their biases, the RED witness, and pre-registration; what SWE-bench, GAIA, WebArena, AgentBench, and τ-bench measure, and what they hide
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development / Survey: SWE-bench (and Verified, Pro), GAIA, WebArena, AgentBench, τ-bench and τ²-bench; LLM-as-judge; the 2026 benchmark breaks · Build: a golden set, a regression delta, and a RED witness wired to a gate (self-guided lab)

The spine is the longest part of the lecture, because each of its sections is a thing you build in this Evolution: a golden set, a delta, a gate, a judge check, a RED witness, and a pre-registered card. The framing comes before the spine; after it come the common mistake, a break, the teardowns, the reference design, the evaluation lens, Flight Card 10, and the lab and Sprint brief. There is no in-class Go/No-Go; your Chase signs the card in the repository before you fly.

Cut from slide 2 (full wording):
- The benchmarks and their graders; SWE-bench Verified retired; the 2026 breaks; MT-Bench as a judge system; Design Analysis of τ²-bench; gzkit eval runner
- Self-guided lab; the Sprint; async Go/No-Go and Chase

Framing. A test that has only ever been green has shown that it runs and nothing more, because a green record cannot distinguish a test that can fail from one that cannot. There are two rules. First, a check counts only after you have seen it fail with the behavior it covers removed; gzkit's glossary calls this the RED witness and defines it as proof that a test fails without the change it covers. Second, you write down what would count as failure before you look at any result; this is pre-registration, and your flight cards have done it since E1. The design claim for this Evolution is the chapter's Sortie 10 claim: the suite fails when it should. Its three falsifiers are the three ways an evaluation suite can report a pass it did not earn, and the fourth line is the rule the reference design learned: a pass obtained by moving the goalposts is a FAIL.

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- Rule one (the RED witness): a check counts only after you have seen it go red. Remove the behavior it covers, run the check, watch it fail, and restore the behavior. / Rule two (pre-registration): write the falsifier before the evidence exists. Commit the threshold, the cases, and the removal diff before the first run.
- Your evaluation suite fails when it should: removing the feature, or planting a wrong answer, turns the gate red. / Three observations falsify it: a green gate with the feature removed; a judge that scores a planted error as correct; a golden case that cannot fail. A pass obtained by editing the golden set or the threshold after the first run counts as a FAIL.

Six words. Task, trial, grader, transcript, and outcome are Anthropic's vocabulary from its January 2026 engineering post on agent evals. I use them because each one points at a different object, and a log that uses one word for two of them is ambiguous. A task is the case; a trial is one attempt at it; the grader scores the trial; the transcript is the record of how the agent got there; the outcome is the state the agent left behind. Anthropic's advice is to grade the outcome rather than the path, because an agent can reach a correct outcome by a valid route the task author did not anticipate. The sixth word is the course's own: a gate is a grader whose result stops something, in other words a grader wired to a command that exits non-zero. An eval that prints a percentage and lets the commit through is a report.

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- One input with a stated success criterion. In a golden set, one line of JSONL with an id, the input, the check, and the expected value.
- One attempt at one task. Model outputs vary between trials, so run a task with a model in the loop more than once.
- The logic that scores a trial: code (equals, contains, schema, a test), a model with a rubric, or a human. One task can carry several graders.
- The full record of a trial: messages, tool calls, intermediate results. Read transcripts. A score alone hides how the agent reached its result.
- The state of the environment after the trial: the row in the database, the file on disk. Where you can, grade the outcome instead of the path.
- The course's addition. The grader's result wired to a command that exits non-zero and stops the build, the commit, or the release. An eval that only prints a number stops nothing, so the course counts it as a report.
- Vocabulary from Anthropic, 'Demystifying evals for AI agents' (Jan 9, 2026). Code graders are fast, cheap, and reproducible. Model graders are flexible and biased. Humans calibrate both.

A golden set is a small set of cases you trust enough to stop the build on. The left panel shows the format I recommend: one JSON object per line, with an id, the requirement it covers, the input, the check, and the expected value. The format has three check types: equals for anything with one right answer, refused for the must-say-no cases, and judge for open answers, with the rubric in a file. The rules on the right follow from the purpose of the set. Draw cases from your failures in AI_LOG rather than from your successes. Tie each case to a requirement. Make a third of them negatives, because an agent that says yes to everything passes a set of positives. Keep the set small enough that you read every failure. Freeze it. Prefer code checks, and send to a judge only what code cannot check, which is why the judge line is last.

Cut from slide 5 (full wording):
- Source. Cases come from AI_LOG and flight-log failures instead of from what the system already does well. / Coverage. Every case cites the requirement it covers. A requirement with no case is untested. A case with no requirement measures nothing the system is required to do. / Negatives. At least a third are must-refuse or must-halt cases. An agent that says yes to everything passes a set made only of positives. / Size. 10–30 cases for a course system. That count covers each requirement twice and keeps the failures few enough to read every one. / Frozen. To change a case after a run, record a ledger event and a reason. A case edited to pass is metagaming (App. C #9). / Deterministic first. Use code checks wherever the answer is checkable. Send only the rest to a judge.

One run is an anecdote. τ-bench, from Yao, Shinn, Razavi, and Narasimhan in June 2024, introduced pass^k, the probability that all k trials of a task succeed. GPT-4o succeeded on fewer than half the tasks, and in the retail domain fewer than a quarter of the tasks passed eight trials out of eight. pass@k rises with k, because it counts any one success among k trials; pass^k falls with k, because it requires every trial to succeed, and pass^k is the rate a user who runs the task every day experiences. The second paragraph draws Anthropic's distinction between two kinds of suite: a capability suite starts low and is meant to climb, and a regression suite sits near a hundred, where any drop is a defect. Your gate is a regression suite. The practical rule for the card: any case with a model in it runs three times, and you report pass^3 beside the mean.

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- pass@k is the chance that at least one of k trials succeeds. It rises with k, so it makes an agent look more reliable than it is. pass^k is the chance that all k succeed. It falls with k, and it matches the experience of a user who runs the task every day. / Two kinds of suite. A capability suite asks what the agent can do. Its pass rate starts low and is meant to climb. A regression suite asks whether the agent still does what it did. Its pass rate sits near 100%, and any drop is a defect. Your Sortie 10 gate is a regression suite with a few capability cases reported beside it. / For your card: run every model-in-the-loop case at least 3 times and report pass^3 alongside the mean.

The gate has five steps. Run every case and write a per-case result. Compare the results against a baseline you froze and committed. Decide with a rule written in code before the first run: any regression, or a rate below the threshold, exits one. Print the ids of the regressed cases, because a red light with no case id sends you to the transcripts blind. Wire the gate into something that runs without you, a hook or CI, because a gate you run by hand when you remember is a report. The strip gives the reason for case-by-case comparison: an aggregate of eighty percent in two successive runs can hide one requirement that broke and another that improved, so the mean hides the regression and only the per-case delta shows it. gzkit's runner has a function called eval_regression_delta for the same reason, and it appears in the reference design teardown.

Cut from slide 7 (full wording):
- Run every case. Write results.json, one pass/fail per case id, plus trial count and model id. / uv run python evals/gate.py
- Load baseline.json (committed, frozen). A regression is a case that passed in the baseline and fails now. The gate reports a new pass, and a new pass does not offset a regression.
- RED if any regression, or if the pass rate is below the pre-registered threshold. The rule is code: / if regressed or rate < THRESHOLD: sys.exit(1)
- Print the ids that regressed and write delta.json. A red gate that does not list the failed case leaves you to search the transcripts for it.
- Call the gate from a pre-commit or pre-push hook, or from CI. A gate that you run by hand only when you remember does not stop the commits you forget to check.
- Why case-by-case: an aggregate can hold steady while one requirement breaks and another improves. The mean can hide the regression. The delta lists the case ids that regressed.

Four biases, each with a paper you can cite in your Design Analysis. Position: Wang and colleagues showed in 2023 that reordering two answers was enough for a weaker model to beat a stronger one on sixty-six of eighty queries. Verbosity: the MT-Bench paper, Zheng and colleagues at NeurIPS 2023, found that judges prefer longer answers, padded ones included. Self-preference: Zheng's paper calls it self-enhancement; Panickssery, Bowman, and Feng showed in 2024 that models recognize their own outputs and that recognition predicts the preference; Wataoka and colleagues argue that the mechanism is familiarity, in other words lower perplexity. Injection is the 2026 addition: the Berkeley group put hidden comments in agent answers and moved the judge's score. The right column is the defense you build for each: judge in both orders, use a binary rubric, judge from a different family, and treat the answer as data, which is the E5 rule applied to the grader.

Cut from slide 8 (full wording):
- Wang et al. (2023), 'Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators': by swapping answer order alone, Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries as judged by an LLM.
- Judge every pair in both orders. Count a verdict only if both orders agree. A flip counts as a tie and goes to a human.
- Zheng et al. (2023) describe self-enhancement bias. Panickssery, Bowman & Feng (2024): models recognize their own text, and self-recognition tracks self-preference. Wataoka et al. (2024): judges favor low-perplexity, familiar text.
- The judge is a different model family from the generator. Strip model names and signatures from what the judge sees.
- Wang, Mang, Cheung, Sen & Song (UC Berkeley, Apr 2026): hidden comments in an agent's answer steered an LLM judge's score (CAR-bench).
- Zheng et al. also found GPT-4 judges agreed with human preferences over 80% of the time, the same rate humans agree with each other. That agreement justifies using a judge. The measured biases require checking the judge before its scores reach a gate.

The RED witness, in one sentence from gzkit's own glossary, is proof that a test fails without the change it covers. The procedure is on the slide: rebuild without the change, run the covering test, expect failure, restore. The idea is older than gzkit. Test-driven development makes you watch the test fail before the code makes it pass; mutation testing, from DeMillo, Lipton, and Sayward in 1978, changes the program on purpose and asks whether the suite notices. An eval suite needs two witnesses: remove the feature, and plant a wrong answer. The third paragraph states what the two catch: a tautological test, where the expected value came from the code under test, and a hollow test, which passes for any output and so never goes red. The lab plants a hollow case. [Verify the gz arb red flags before class.]

Cut from slide 10 (full wording):
- Where the idea comes from. Test-driven development writes the test first and watches it fail (red) before the code makes it pass (green). Mutation testing (DeMillo, Lipton & Sayward, 1978) generalizes it: change the program on purpose; a suite that still passes has not tested what changed. gzkit calls the recorded version a RED witness and runs it with gz arb red. [Verify the command's current flags against the repository before class.] / For an eval suite, two witnesses. (1) Feature removed: comment out the behavior. The cases that cover it must go red, and you must have predicted which ones before the run. (2) Wrong answer planted: substitute one wrong output. The grader or judge must fail it. / What it catches. A tautological test compares the code with itself (expected value computed by the function under test). A hollow test passes for any output (assert result is not None; a check that accepts every label). Both stay green on every run and still count toward coverage.

Pre-registration is the flight card's origin outside aviation. Nosek and colleagues, in PNAS in 2018, put the distinction as prediction versus postdiction: a hypothesis fixed before the data tests something, and a hypothesis fitted after the data only describes it. Kerr's 1998 paper gave the failure its label, HARKing, hypothesizing after the results are known. In an eval suite, HARKing looks like choosing the threshold after the score, dropping the failing case, re-running until green, or padding the set with cases the system already passes. The course's mechanism against it has three parts: commit the card and the golden set first, put the commit hash on the card, and have the Chase sign that commit. The strip is the test to apply to every card: could the evidence have come out against you, and did you say in advance what that would look like?

Cut from slide 11 (full wording):
- State the hypothesis, the measure, and the decision rule before observing the outcome. Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven & Mellor (PNAS, 2018): pre-registration separates prediction, which tests a claim, from postdiction, which only generates one.
- HARKing, hypothesizing after the results are known (Kerr, 1998). In evals: choosing the threshold after seeing the score; dropping the case that failed; re-running until green; adding a case the system already passes.
- The card holds the claim, the threshold, the case count, the removal diff, and the falsifiers. Commit it and the golden set before the first run, and write the commit hash on the card. The Chase signs that commit. Amendments are appended with a reason and never overwrite earlier entries.
- To test a pre-registration, ask two questions: could the evidence have come out against you, and did you state in advance what that result would look like?

The common mistake for this Evolution. If you record the agent's current output as the expected value, you build the set in minutes, and the set is green on day one and blind to every bug present on that day. Such a set detects change, which has some value, and it never checked correctness, because no one compared the recorded output with the requirement. Its cousins are the not-None assertion, the judge asked whether an answer is good with no reference, and a fixture that mocks the thing under test. On the board: remove the feature, and some snapshot cases do go red; then plant a bug that was present on snapshot day, and nothing goes red, because the golden recorded the bug. The rule for Sortie 10 follows: expected values come from requirements, written by hand before the agent runs.

Cut from slide 12 (full wording):
- Common mistake: goldens copied from the system's own output
- for case in inputs: /     case['expect'] = agent(case['input'])  # 'record the golden' / json.dump(cases, open('golden.json', 'w')) / The set now encodes whatever the agent did on the day you ran it, bugs included. Every case passes on the first run. It will catch a change, but not a wrong behavior that was already there, and nobody checked whether the output was right. / Related failures: assert result is not None; a judge asked 'is this a good answer?'; a fixture that mocks the feature under test.
- 1. Take the snapshot set. Remove the feature. Some cases go red, as they should. / 2. Now plant a bug that was present on snapshot day (the agent always called a write tool 'write', even for delete). Nothing goes red, because the golden says 'write'. / 3. Fix: write expected values from the requirement, by hand, before running the agent. Snapshots are allowed only as a change detector, labeled as such, beside the golden set. / Rule for Sortie 10: every expected value in golden.jsonl traces to a requirement or an AI_LOG entry, and no expected value comes from a run.

The judge as a system. MT-Bench is eighty multi-turn questions graded by GPT-4; Chatbot Arena collects crowdsourced pairwise votes between anonymous models. The design choice replaces human raters with a model, and the paper justifies it by agreement: GPT-4 matched human preference above eighty percent of the time, which equals the rate at which humans agree with each other. The cost is that the judge's biases enter every score, and the paper measured three of them: position, verbosity, and self-enhancement. The failure mode is metagaming at scale: a system tuned against a judge learns the judge's preferences. The strip is the habit I want in your Design Analysis: when you cite this paper for the eighty percent, cite it for the biases as well.

Cut from slide 17 (full wording):
- Teardown: MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, the judge as a system
- 80 multi-turn questions (MT-Bench) graded by GPT-4 as judge, in single-answer and pairwise modes; Chatbot Arena collects crowd votes between two anonymous models. 3K expert votes and 30K conversations released.
- The method replaces human raters with a strong model, because humans are slow and costly. The authors justify the replacement by agreement: GPT-4 matched human preference over 80% of the time, the same as human-human agreement.
- The judge's biases enter every score: position, verbosity, self-enhancement, limited reasoning on math. The paper measured them and proposed swaps and reference answers; a user of the method can skip both, and the scores then carry the biases.
- App. C #9 at scale: a system tuned against a judge learns the judge's preferences. Longer, more confident answers score higher whether or not they are right. Defense: the judge admissibility checks (Blind, Binary, Calibrated, Planted).

The live Design Analysis. The class fills the nine components in on the board, and this slide is the answer key. Three rows carry the design decisions. Tools: in the telecom domain the user also has tools, which is what dual control means, so the agent must get a person to act rather than acting itself. Evaluation: the grader compares the final database with the goal state, which is outcome grading, and pass^k measures consistency across trials. Governance: a model simulates the human, so the benchmark has a model inside its own grading path, and any simulator error lands on the agent's score. The judgment loop is in the strip; write your own before you read mine.

- Agent tools on the backend; in telecom, the user also has tools on their own device (dual control, modeled as a Dec-POMDP).
- Agent and user must coordinate: the agent guides a user who acts. Ablations separate reasoning errors from communication errors.
- Final database state compared with the goal state; pass^k over repeated trials. The grader checks the outcome and ignores the transcript.
- The human is simulated, and the simulator is a model: its errors enter the agent's score.

Evolution 11 is the second of the two evaluation Evolutions. In Evolution 10 the gate went red when a feature was removed. In this Evolution the question is what the system did when somebody tried to make it misbehave, and how you know what it did. The framing phrase is receipts over narrative: a record the system wrote outranks any account of the run, the model's or yours. The survey reads two 2026 frontier system cards for their agentic sections, a 2026 prompt-injection disclosure that hit three vendors' coding agents at once, three observability stacks, and the two OWASP lists. The build puts tracing on your own loop, adds a cost table, and tests your guardrails against five pre-registered attacks, two of them written by your Chase. The lab is the same exercise at its smallest size: one attack, one guardrail, one exported trace.

The book's thesis sentence is on the slide: a system can produce an answer without being able to answer for it. In this Evolution that sentence becomes two rules. Rule one: the black box outranks the narrative. The model's account of what it did is a claim, your summary of the run is a claim, and only a trace or a receipt is evidence, because only those two records were written by the mechanism that acted rather than by a party describing it. Rule two: a guardrail is a mechanism at an enforcement locus, in other words a place in the harness where the system can refuse (a permission deny, a server-side check, a commit-time check), and it earns credit only when a delivered attack reached it and the trace shows the refusal. Sortie 11 tests the chapter's design claim: your system survives five pre-registered attacks without a write, a leak, or a false attestation. The claim's third falsifier is the one the common-mistake slide returns to: an attack the system never received proves nothing about the guardrail, so a guardrail credited for such an attack fails the sortie, and so does a pass obtained by disabling a check.

The black box holds four kinds of record, and each answers a different question. A trace is a tree of spans for one run: the agent invocation at the top, with the model calls and tool calls under it, each timed and carrying attributes. A receipt is narrower and stricter. It records the observed result of one command (the exit status, the duration, the git state, and the tail of stdout) and validates against a schema. Because it records the git state, a receipt binds a result to a commit. The ledger is the project's runtime truth, the append-only log of what was decided, attested, and closed, and by whom. The transcript is what the model said, and it is evidence of nothing the model claims to have done: the model's sentence 'I did not read the env file' is a claim, and the tool span for the read is the evidence. The lab has you check the one against the other.

What a trace may hold falls into three columns. Always log the metadata: which operation, which model, which tool, what status, how long it took, what it cost, on which commit, and which guardrail refused. Log content (prompt and response text, tool arguments and results, system instructions) only by a decision recorded in the ADR, per sortie, and prefer a hash or a truncation when the Chase needs only to know which document was read. Never log secrets, credential files, or personal data, and that rule includes data about you. The trace store is part of the attack surface for the reason the strip states: an attacker who makes the agent print a secret has caused one leak, and a logger that writes that output to disk causes a second. The reference design learned this in April 2026 with a history rewrite, which the incident slide returns to. The canary is the test: a fake value that contains a unique string, and a search of every committed file for that string, where any hit is a leak.

The numbers are a worked example rather than a measurement, and the slide says so. One sortie of forty turns sends about 1.2 million input tokens, because the loop re-sends the context every turn, and produces about eighteen thousand output tokens. At the Go list price for GLM-5.3 Flash as of September 2026, the model bill is nineteen cents. Forty-five minutes of your attention at an assumed fifty dollars an hour is thirty-seven dollars and fifty cents. The per-turn numbers hold two traps. Cached reads sit inside the input count, so a table that multiplies input tokens by the list price overstates the cost when the cache is warm. Go limits are denominated in dollars per five hours, per week, and per month, so your cost table also predicts when the provider will stop you.

An attack card has five fields, and you write it before you fly, as a flight card is written before a sortie. The objective is one sentence the attacker wants to be true, and it becomes your falsifier. Delivery states how the payload reaches the loop, and the payload's SHA-256 lets the Chase find that exact payload in your trace without taking your word that it was delivered. The guardrail field states a mechanism and the locus where it enforces; if the answer is 'the system prompt tells it not to', the card has no guardrail. The expected observable is the span or receipt that will show the refusal. The falsifiers include the chapter's third: a guardrail credited because the payload never arrived. The strip describes trust-chain poisoning, the attack in which no single step is wrong because each layer accepted the layer below as fact, and for this reason one of your five attacks is delivered through a tool result.

- In trust-chain poisoning, no single step is bad: each layer accepts the output of the layer below as fact. Write one card whose delivery is a tool result, not a user turn.

A system card is the lab's evaluation report on the model: what the lab tested, how, with which outside evaluators, and which safety threshold the lab placed the model under. It cannot evaluate your harness, because your tools, permissions, data, and prompts were not in the lab's test. A card's 96% injection resistance is a rate across the lab's attacks, and your system meets the other 4% with what you built. The translation from card to guardrail is mechanical, and your attack card records it: a finding becomes a mode, the mode becomes an attack, and the attack states the guardrail under test. Where the guardrail sits decides whether the model can talk its way past it, so order the candidates by what the model cannot argue with: a permission deny the harness enforces, a scope check on the server, a hook, a check on git diff --cached at commit time. The strip states how to read the tables in the teardowns: the rate that remains after the lab's mitigations is the rate your harness inherits, so the remainder is your threat model.

The common mistake is a log that reads 'all five attacks failed', written from the model's final message and an unchanged file. The black box tells a different story. Two payloads never entered the loop, because the injected file sat outside the directory the agent searched, and the model refused a third before any tool ran, so the guardrail the card listed was never exercised and has no refusal span. Model refusal is a real outcome, and you record it, but it is a property of this model on this day, and the next model may comply. Only the guardrail stops an attack the model does not refuse. For this reason each attack needs two pieces of evidence, the delivery span and the refusal span or receipt, and a model refusal is recorded as 'refused by model; guardrail not exercised' with a variant flown that reaches the guardrail.

Comment and Control is a disclosure by Aonan Guan and colleagues at Johns Hopkins, published April 15, 2026: one prompt-injection pattern against three vendors' coding agents running in GitHub Actions, and in each case the agent's own credentials left the loop. Claude Code's security reviewer interpolated the pull-request title into its prompt, ran a process listing through Bash that exposed its keys, and posted them in a PR comment. Gemini's CLI action followed a fake 'trusted content' section planted in an issue comment and posted its API key as a public issue comment. Copilot's coding agent read an HTML comment that the rendered issue hides, base64-encoded the process listing so that secret scanning would not match, and committed the result through the one channel it was allowed to use. The mechanism is the same in all three: untrusted text reached a loop that held secrets and a write path. Guan's root cause is that pairing, and his defense is an allowlist of tools and secrets, because a blocklist fails by substitution (deny ps and the attacker reads /proc instead). VentureBeat's report adds that Anthropic's Opus 4.7 card had already stated that the security-review action was not hardened against injection.

Cut from slide 15 (full wording):
- Enters: an HTML comment in an issue body, invisible when rendered. / Acts: ps auxeww | base64, which evades secret scanning. / Leaves: encoded credentials in a git commit, pushed through an allowed channel.
- Aonan Guan's root cause: the agent holds production secrets because it needs them, and processes untrusted input because that is its job. His defense: allowlists of tools and secrets in place of blocklists.

Langfuse, LangSmith, and the OpenCode export are three ways to hold the black box, each read for the design choice it made. Langfuse is open source under the MIT licence, is built on OpenTelemetry, and defines a guardrail observation type, which shows that its designers expected a guardrail refusal to appear in a trace. It joined ClickHouse in January 2026 and states that the licence is not changing. LangSmith is proprietary and hosted, accepts OTLP, and groups traces into threads by a metadata key that every child run must carry, or the cost roll-up for the thread is wrong. OpenCode has no tracing product, but its session export already holds the facts a hosted stack would: which tool, what status, how long, what it cost. The failure modes differ by where the data goes. Each stack stores whatever content you send it, so a secret that passes into content is mode 8 at the store, and with LangSmith the trace leaves your machine. OpenCode's share command publishes a session at a public URL until you unshare it. The lab uses the export and sets share to disabled for both reasons.

OWASP maintains two lists that apply here. The Top 10 for LLM Applications is still the 2025 edition, and the Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 was released on December 9, 2025. The LLM list describes what goes wrong in one model call: injection, disclosure, output handling, excessive agency. The agentic list describes what goes wrong in a loop: goal hijack, tool misuse, privilege abuse, memory poisoning, inter-agent communication, cascading failures. Map your system to both. The two lists differ from the nine modes in direction: OWASP lists what an attacker does to the system, and Appendix C lists what the agent does wrong in response, so an attack card cites one entry of each. ASI08, cascading failures, is trust-chain poisoning under OWASP's label, and the reference design's April outage is an instance of it.

Appendix G, the gzkit incident casebook, supplies three dated incidents, each a mode from Appendix C with a mechanism you can copy. On April 19, personal data about the operator ended up in committed artifacts, and the only fix was a history rewrite. Evolution 12 is the last lecture. Through eleven Evolutions your system has worked on your laptop while you watched it. In this Evolution it becomes a system that runs when you are not watching, and one that you can take back when it goes wrong. As used in this lecture, a system is operated when someone other than its author can release it, see which version is live, and roll it back from a written page. The survey covers the background agents that the vendors now run for you in the cloud and on a schedule, and reads each one for who attests an unattended run. The build serves, packages, releases, and rolls back your system, with the rollback in the ledger. Code freeze and the closeout ceremonies follow this Evolution on the dates in the course calendar.

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- Evolution 12 · Lecture
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development / Survey: background and cloud agents (Codex cloud, Copilot cloud agent, Claude Code cloud sessions, routines, and GitHub Actions) · gzkit closeout, patch release, MX   ·   Build: your system served, packaged, released, and rolled back in one governed command / Code freeze, then closeout ceremonies

The lecture runs in seven segments: framing, the spine in two halves, a break, the teardowns with one Design Analysis on the board, the reference design, and the lens, the card, the ceremony, and the lab. There is no Go/No-Go in the room for this Evolution. Your Chase signs your card in the repository by the date in the course calendar, as in the previous Sorties.

Working means the system ran for you, on your machine, while you watched. Operated means a second person can release it, tell which version is live, and roll it back from a written page. The lecture adds two rules. First, a release is an artifact with a version and a hash, and a rollback reinstalls that artifact. If your rollback is to check out the old tag and rebuild, you are releasing a new, untested artifact that happens to share a version number, and I will show you the two hashes later in the lecture. Second, the process receives its secrets at run time, and they appear nowhere else, the model's context included. Sortie 12 tests the design claim from chapter twenty-one with one addition: the rollback must record the same hash that was released. The last falsifier belongs to the Heavy lane: a release with no attestation event does not count as a release.

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- The release is a built artifact (a wheel or an image) that carries a version and a hash. Rollback reinstalls an artifact that already exists and never rebuilds from an old commit. / The deploy environment injects secrets at run time: the key reaches the process from the environment. The key never appears in the image, the log, the repository, or the model's context.
- A release of your system can be rolled back in one governed command; the rollback is in the ledger and records the same artifact hash that was released; and a planted canary secret appears in no image layer, log, or commit. / Falsifiers: a rollback that needs a manual step; a rollback whose hash differs from the release it restores; the canary found in any artifact; a release with no attestation event.

Chapter twenty-one, section one, distinguishes two ways to serve an agent: as a service or as a job. You choose between them before you choose a framework. A service has a waiting caller, so it needs a time budget, an idempotency key, streaming for long answers, and a health route. A job has no waiting caller, so it needs a budget in turns and dollars, an artifact as its output, and an exit code the scheduler can read. A job that you wrap as a service for the demo is an acceptable design if the ADR says so. The failure to avoid is the service with job semantics: a long loop behind a POST, a client that times out and retries, and three copies of the agent spending your budget on the same task.

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- A caller sends a request and waits. FastAPI or an equivalent in front of your loop. / Every request has a time budget; the loop halts inside it / An idempotency key keeps a retried POST from running the agent twice / Long answers stream; the client sees progress / /health reports status and version
- A trigger starts a run; nobody waits on a socket. A CLI entry point, a cron line, a scheduled cloud agent. / The run has a turn budget and a dollar budget in place of a request timeout / Output is an artifact: a branch, a report, a ledger entry / A person reads the result later, so the result must state what the run did / Exit code is the only status the scheduler sees
- A course system can be a job that a student wraps as a service for the demo. Either lifecycle is acceptable. Pick one in an ADR and state the lifecycle. / The failure case is a service with job semantics: a POST that starts a ten-minute loop, a client that times out at 60 seconds and retries, and three agents doing the same work with your key.
- A request that outlives its caller becomes an orphan. Decide which mechanism halts the run: the loop's budget or the server's timeout.

The served agent is thirty lines, and each line carries a decision from the previous slide. The per-turn timeout (TURN_TIMEOUT_S) comes from the environment. The lifespan handler reads the API key at startup, so a missing key stops the process at boot instead of at the first request; that is Nygard's Fail Fast pattern. The health route returns the installed version, which is how you will see a rollback from outside the process. The run route takes an idempotency key as a header, so a client retry returns the first result instead of starting a second agent, and it wraps the loop in a timeout, so the halt happens inside the caller's budget and the caller gets a 504 that says so. I ran this file with the test client: a repeated key calls the loop once, a slow task returns 504, and a missing key header returns 422. The idempotency store is in memory, so state that limit in your runbook.

Five concerns appear in the table, each with a wrong place, a right place, and a check a peer can run without your help. The row to slow down on is secrets. An ENV line or a COPY of a dot-env file in a Dockerfile puts the key into an image layer, and every pull of that image carries it; a later layer that deletes the file does not remove it from the history. Inject the key at run time from an untracked file or a secret store, and check with a canary, in other words a fake key with a unique string that you plant in your environment and then search for in the image history, the logs, and the git log. The provider's rate limit does not protect your budget. Your system needs its own budget per run and per key, and exceeding that budget on purpose is a test point. The note on the slide is FastAPI's own container guidance.

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- FastAPI's container guidance: one process per container; use the exec form of CMD so lifespan shutdown runs; add --proxy-headers behind a TLS proxy (fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker).
- A secret in any layer of an image is in every copy of that image forever. Deleting it in a later layer does not remove it.

There are two ways to ship the same release, and the lab offers both because laptops differ. The left panel uses uv's own commands: bump the version, build a wheel into dist, and install it into a separate environment that stands in for production. Rollback reinstalls the prior wheel, and the wheel's hash is in the release record. The right panel ships an image. The point to take from that panel is that a tag is a pointer, and the next docker build with the same tag moves it, so the image ID or the registry digest is the release. Both panels end on the same rule: a version number is only a name, so record the hash when you release and check it when you roll back.

Cut from slide 7 (full wording):
- uv version --bump patch   → pyproject says 0.1.1 / uv build   → dist/myagent-0.1.1-py3-none-any.whl (and an sdist) / Install into a deploy environment that stands in for production: uv venv deploy-env, then uv pip install the wheel into it. / Rollback: reinstall the prior wheel file from the release record. The release record holds the wheel's SHA-256; the rollback checks it before it installs. / This path needs no daemon and no admin rights, so a standard student laptop can run it.
- docker build -t myagent:0.1.1 .  (or podman build) / The tag is a pointer. The image ID (or the registry digest) is the release. Record the ID in the release event, because a tag can be moved to a different image by the next build. / Rollback: stop the running container and start the prior image by ID or by a tag you have verified still points at that ID. / This path needs Docker or Podman. Some laptops cannot run either, so the lab does not require this path.
- A version number is a label that a later build can reuse; the hash identifies the release. Record the hash when you release and check it when you roll back.

Section three of the chapter asks who attests an unattended run. The vendors in the teardown table ship the same five controls in some form, and you will see each control in the teardowns. The first is a stored trigger, which proves that somebody wrote the prompt earlier and proves nothing about whether this run's actions were approved. The second is an isolated environment with the network limited by default. The third is a narrow write path: one branch with a prefix, and no merge by the agent. The fourth is a human merge. The fifth is a record that someone reads, because a green status says only that the process exited; Anthropic's routines documentation states that last point in so many words. For your system the rule is this: if you schedule anything, the scheduled run writes to its own branch or its own file, a person accepts it, and the ledger shows both events.

Cut from slide 8 (full wording):
- The prompt and schedule are written ahead of time by an authorized person. The firing shows only that the prompt was stored, and it gives no consent for this run's actions.
- One branch with a known prefix (copilot/, claude/, codex/). No push to a protected branch; no merge by the agent.
- A run log exists. A green status means only that the run exited. A person reads the transcript to decide whether the task succeeded.
- Fresh VM or runner per run; network limited by default; secrets held outside the sandbox where the vendor supports it.
- Nobody watched the run, so the run's record must answer three questions: what did it change, under whose authority, and who accepted it.

Nygard's second edition of Release It!, 2018, is on the reading list, and the slide takes six cards from its stability chapters that map onto an agent loop. Timeouts go on every call, and Nygard advises against an immediate retry, because the fault is probably still there when the timeout fires. A Circuit Breaker guards a flaky provider, with the breaker's state visible in health. Steady State requires that every store that grows has a purge, and the idempotency store in the served agent is the example to check. Fail Fast is what you saw in the lifespan handler. The last two speak directly to automation. Force Multiplier is the antipattern: automation that spreads one bad decision everywhere, and a scheduled agent is that automation. Governor is the answer: resistance in the unsafe direction, so that a person can step in. The Governor is the confirmation gate you built in Evolution 3, applied to deployment.

Cut from slide 9 (full wording):
- Every model call and tool call has one. Nygard: do not retry at once after a timeout; the fault is probably still there. Queue or halt.
- After N failures from a provider or tool, stop calling it for a period and fail the run with a reason. Expose the breaker's state in /health.
- Check the key, the model route, and the budget before the first turn, so that a run that cannot finish never starts.
- Slow automation down in the unsafe direction so a human can intervene: deletes, deploys, mass writes need a pause and a person.
- Automation that amplifies one wrong decision across the fleet. A background agent on a schedule is a force multiplier for whatever its prompt gets wrong.
- The Governor is the pattern the course has been building since E3: a write needs a confirmation event, and an irreversible act needs a human.

Through the term you ran the Lite lane, gates one and two, the ADR and the tests. The Final System runs the Heavy lane, and the slide lists the three gates a release adds. Gate 3 is docs: the docs describe the release that exists, and the test is to paste every command from the runbook. Gate 4 is BDD: scenarios for the contract a caller relies on, and the scenarios run. Gate 5 is human: an attestation event in the ledger with one of three words, recorded by you. You have seen the reference design's incidents in which an agent recorded an attestation that nobody gave; for this reason the agent never records Gate 5. The last card separates two documents: the changelog is for maintainers, and the release notes are for the person who has to upgrade or roll back.

Cut from slide 10 (full wording):
- The README, the runbook, and the release notes describe the release that exists. A command in the docs that fails when pasted is a gate failure.
- Scenarios for the external contract: what a caller of /runs, or a user of the CLI, can rely on. Given, when, then, and each scenario runs as a test.
- A person attests: Completed, Completed — Partial, or Dropped. The attestation is an event in the ledger. The agent never records it for you.
- The changelog is every change, for maintainers. Release notes are what a user must know to upgrade and to roll back. Both state the version and the date.
- Chapter 21.5: docs gate; BDD for external contracts; human attestation; release notes vs. changelog; the distribution invariant; MX mode. The reference design segment covers the last two.

The common mistake is rollback by rebuild, and I made it on purpose while I wrote the lab. I built version 0.1.0, released it, and recorded its hash. Then I set the version back and built again, which is what a rollback by rebuild does. The result was the same file name, the same version string, and different bytes; the first eight characters of the two hashes are on the slide. The rollback installed the new file, health reported 0.1.0, and only the hash showed that the running artifact differed from the released one. In my run the smoke test caught the difference because the code had changed; a subtle change would have passed the smoke test and left the hash as the only evidence. The fix is in the strip, and it is step four of the lab: keep released artifacts out of the build's reach, and make the rollback compare hashes.

Cut from slide 11 (full wording):
- What happened. The version was set back to 0.1.0 and uv build ran again. The new wheel overwrote the old one at the same path. The rollback installed it, and the ledger recorded a rollback to 0.1.0 with a hash that did not match the release it claimed to restore. / Why it passes a careless check. The version string is right, the file name is right, and health reports 0.1.0. Only the hash shows that the running wheel differs from the released wheel.
- Keep every released artifact where a build cannot overwrite it, and make the rollback refuse a hash that differs from the release event.

The runbook in the Sprint is one page with seven sections, and the right-hand column of the table states how your Chase tests each section without asking you anything. The two sections that matter most are rollback, with the time you measured and what the command refuses to do, and known gaps, where you write down what the runbook does not cover. Chapter twenty-one's exercise is the same task: roll back your own release, time it, and put the number in the runbook.

Five systems appear in the table, read for runtime and governance. Codex cloud runs a container per task, runs your setup script with network access, and then blocks the network in the agent phase by default. GitHub renamed Copilot's agent from coding agent to cloud agent on April first; it runs in an ephemeral Actions environment with a 59-minute cap, behind a firewall, and it can push only to its own branch. Claude Code's cloud sessions run in an isolated VM with a network allowlist by default; routines are the scheduled and triggered form, hourly at the most frequent, and they push to claude-prefixed branches as your GitHub identity. The GitHub Action is the agent as a CI job, so it inherits whatever permissions and secrets the workflow has. Across all five systems, the agent never merges.

Instructor checks moved off the slide:
- [Verify every cell before class; these pages change monthly.]

The Copilot cloud agent teardown reads for the four headings every teardown uses: mechanism, design choice, cost, and failure mode. The mechanism is that a task arrives, the agent runs in an Actions environment you can prepare with a setup-steps workflow, and it pushes to one branch and opens a draft pull request. The design choice places the human gate in the pull request, where developers already work, and denies the agent every action that would close that gate itself: no ready-for-review, no approve, no merge, and no CI run until a person approves it. The cost is Actions minutes, AI credits, and review load. The failure modes are metagaming the gate, in other words a PR that satisfies the checks but not the task, and safeguard circumvention if the agent can edit the workflow that checks it. The strip states the attribution rule: the commits carry the assigner as co-author, which records who asked, and only the review records who checked.

Cut from slide 15 (full wording):
- A task arrives from an issue, a panel, or a PR comment. The agent works in an ephemeral Actions environment prepared by .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml (the job must be called copilot-setup-steps, and the file must sit on the default branch). It pushes to one copilot/ branch and opens a draft PR.
- Put the human gate where developers already look: the pull request. Only users with write access can start it. The agent cannot mark its PR ready, approve, or merge. Actions workflows on its PR do not run until a person clicks Approve and run workflows.

CIDM6333_E1_Lecture_AgentLoop.pptx:
Evolution 1. Evolution 0 gave you maps and a posture. This Evolution gives you the loop, the smallest unit an agent is built from. Every later Evolution adds tools, memory, coordination, or evaluation to this loop, which is the reason an hour on its exact shape is a sound investment. The framing sentence for this Evolution is that a loop without a halt is a bill. The survey covers ReAct, then AutoGPT and BabyAGI, then the genesis of the reference design. The build is a governed loop that halts, with a PRD attested. [0:00–0:01]

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- Evolution 1 · Lecture
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development / Survey: ReAct · AutoGPT/BabyAGI · gzkit genesis   ·   Build: a governed loop that halts; PRD attested

The lecture makes five moves. The framing comes first. The spine comes second and gets the most time, because the spine is the build. Two teardowns follow, done live against the nine components. The reference design comes fourth, and the evaluation lens with the card brief closes the hour. The consultation afterward takes your pitch in one sentence and your E0 Design Analysis, defended.

The lesson comes before the history. A loop with no stop condition keeps calling the model provider until a human intervenes, so the provider keeps billing, and nobody has settled who is responsible for what the loop did in the meantime. Evolution 0 established that the model has no state, no ground truth, and no accountability. The loop is the first structure the builder puts around the model, and the loop inherits those gaps unless the builder designs against them. A budget is the first piece of state, an observation is the first piece of ground truth, and a ledger is the first piece of accountability. Then read the design claim for this Evolution aloud, because every design claim in the course takes its shape: one sentence, and beside it the falsifiers that would disprove it (three, on this card). [~8 min]

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- An agent loop with no stop condition keeps spending on the model provider's account, and it leaves open who is responsible for what the agent did.
- A language model has no persistent state, no ground truth, and no accountability. The loop is the first structure a designer puts around the model, and the loop inherits all three gaps unless the design closes each one: a budget closes the state gap, an observation closes the ground-truth gap, and a ledger closes the accountability gap.
- The design claim Sortie 1 will try to disprove / The loop halts on every input class (answerable, unanswerable, adversarial) within budget, and every turn is in the ledger. If a single run exceeds the turn budget, halts with no ledger event, or produces a 'final answer' without a reasoning turn, the design claim is false.

The prompt became a control structure in four steps over two years. With few-shot prompting, the examples in the prompt steer the completion, so the prompt works as data. With chain-of-thought, the model emits its reasoning as text, so you can read it, and latent planning appears in that text. With self-consistency, the builder samples several chains and takes a vote, which is the first evaluator and also the first time cost multiplies, by the sample count. With ReAct, the prompt interleaves reasoning with actions and observations, so the prompt is now a loop body. Chain-of-thought plans without commitment, because no step checks the reasoning against the world. ReAct adds the observation, so each reasoning step carries a piece of ground truth, and that one addition turns a generative system into an agent. [~5 min]

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- In chain-of-thought prompting the model reasons and then answers, and nothing checks the reasoning against the world. /  / ReAct adds the observation. After each action the environment answers back, and the next reasoning step has ground truth in it. /  / This course uses the observation inside the loop as the line between a generative system and an agent: an agent's next reasoning step depends on what the environment returned.
- Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022) / 'Let's think step by step' (Kojima et al., 2022). The model emits its reasoning as text a person can read, and planning that was latent becomes visible.

Read the ReAct paper as a design document. The slide shows a trace in the paper's format: thought, action, observation, thought, action, finish. Work through the nine components with the room. The component map on the right holds the answers. Four of the components deserve attention. The tools are a fixed and small set, declared in the prompt. The memory is the trace and nothing else. Evaluation sits entirely outside the loop, on benchmarks, so no step inside the loop checks a thought. Governance consisted of the human who wrote the prompt and then left. The halt is the finish action, and nothing forces the loop to call it. ReAct lacked memory, a budget, and verification, and each of those three is a later Evolution. [~5 min]
