- Foundation  PaLM-540B / GPT-3 era, hosted / Perception  the question + prior observations / Planning  free-text thoughts between actions / Tools  a fixed, tiny set (search, lookup, finish) / Memory  the trace itself; nothing beyond the window / Coordination  single agent / Evaluation  none inside the loop; benchmarks outside / Governance  the human wrote the prompt, then left / Runtime  a script; halt = the finish action /  / ReAct lacked memory, a budget, and verification. Later Evolutions add each one.

The build fits in a dozen lines, and the slide reads top to bottom. The loop starts with a message list. A bounded for-loop supplies the first halt. A model call returns a structured Step, so the decision is typed, and the parser rejects a malformed decision instead of the loop executing it. The loop appends every turn to the ledger before it does anything else with the turn. If the step is an answer, the loop halts. If the step is a tool, the loop calls the tool and puts the observation back into the messages. The loop then checks the cost budget. If the turns run out, the loop raises, and it never returns silently. That gives four halts, and the ledger records each one with a reason. You will run this loop twice, once against your hosted route and once against Ollama, and measure the difference. Some small models cannot produce the schema at all. That result is a finding about the model, so record it in the flight log rather than treating it as a bug in your loop. [~5 min]

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- The loop parses each model output into Step, a Pydantic model with the fields kind ∈ {answer, tool}, name, args, and text. A malformed decision cannot reach the loop: the parser rejects it, and the rejection goes back to the model as an observation.
- Final answer · turn budget · cost budget · error. The loop writes each halt to the ledger with its reason, so the Chase can tell a correct halt from an exit that left no record.
- Run the same loop against a hosted API and against Ollama's endpoint. For each run, measure latency, cost, and whether the small model can produce the schema at all.

Five failures appear on day one, and each one maps to a falsifier or an abort on your card. When the loop never halts because the model never emits an answer, the turn budget stops it, and a check for repeated identical actions stops it sooner. When a tool raises and the loop swallows the exception, treat the error as an observation and halt once the error count passes a limit. When a small model cannot produce the schema, retry within a retry budget, then halt with the reason format, and log the case as a squawk rather than as a failure of the design. When the model answers with no reasoning turn before it, that run trips a falsifier on the card. When an adversarial input asks the loop to ignore its budget, the loop halts anyway, because the budget lives in code and the prompt cannot reach it. The rule for the semester follows from the last case: the model can argue past a budget stated only in the prompt, so code enforces every budget and the ledger records every halt. [~5 min]

- Halt conditions, budgets, and what goes wrong on day one
- Rule for the semester: code enforces every budget, because the model can argue its way past a budget that exists only in the prompt. Halts live in code and in the ledger, never only in the prompt.

The second teardown is AutoGPT, and this one goes on the board with the room. AutoGPT's loop takes a goal in one sentence. The model writes a task list, executes one task with search or files or code, rewrites the list from its own summary of what it did, and goes around again. The only halt was a human closing the terminal or the API key running dry. Ask the room which component was absent. Evaluation was absent, because no step checked a result before that result fed the next plan, and the model graded itself from its own summary (summary laundering, in an early form). Governance was absent, because the goal had no performance measure, no halt, and no attestation. Memory was a vector store of the model's own outputs, so a hallucinated fact came back later as retrieved truth. Planning was present and fluent, and the fluency is the uncomfortable part, because a model that writes fluent plans with no grounding produces a spiral that reads as progress from inside. AutoGPT mattered for two reasons. It stated the ambition (give a model a goal and let it run), and it gave the field its first shared record of failure. The evaluators, budgets, and human-in-the-loop designs of 2024 and 2025 reply to that spring. [~8 min]

Cut from slide 8 (full wording):
- The loop with goals and no grounding, no budget, no evaluator: why it spiraled
- AutoGPT stated the ambition plainly: give a model a goal and let it run. The repository gathered hundreds of thousands of GitHub stars in weeks. /  / It also produced the field's first shared record of failures: loops that spent budget on the same task, rewrote plans in circles, and reported progress that had not happened. /  / The 2024–25 designs this course covers (evaluators, budgets, human-in-the-loop, workflows over agents) each answer a failure from that spring. /  / Judgment loop: decision = full autonomy from a goal; privileged = ambition and demo value; cost = grounding; failure mode = spiral; preservation = none (by design).
- Which of the nine components was absent, and which absence caused the spiral? / Evaluation: nothing checked a task's result before it fed the next plan; the model graded itself from its own summary. / Governance: the goal was one sentence; no performance measure (PEAS's P), no halt, no attestation. / Memory: a vector store of its own outputs, so the agent retrieved its own hallucinated 'facts' as truth. / Planning was present and fluent. Because nothing grounded the plans, each new plan read well while the task made no progress.

The table puts the two side by side. In one year the loop gained an explicit plan, an open tool set, a vector memory, spawned subagents, and a daemon runtime, and it gained nothing in evaluation or governance. The reason sits in what the authors of each system built it to show. ReAct's authors built it to show that reasoning and acting improve each other, so it optimized for a benchmark and left everything else out. AutoGPT's authors built it to show that a goal is enough, so it optimized for ambition and left grounding out. Both lacked a budget, an evaluator, and a record. The operator started the reference design in January 2026 to fill that gap, two more years after the 2023 spring, and the delay shows how long the field took to act on the lesson. Your Design Analysis for this Evolution is one of these two systems. Write the one I did not do on the board. [~7 min]

- Same loop, one year apart: what changed, and what was missing in both
- ReAct's authors built it to show that reasoning and acting improve each other, so it optimized for a benchmark and left everything else out. AutoGPT's developers built it to show that a goal alone can drive a loop, and they gave it no grounding. /  / Both lacked a budget, an evaluator, and a record. gzkit, the system on the next slide, was started in January 2026 to close that gap, after two more years of the same failure.

The reference design began as the loop plus the thing the loop lacked. On January 12th, eleven days before the operator would show the system to students, the model said that only specification matters. The operator refused: specification, methodology, and governance, all three, or the loop drifts. [Verify the quote against genesis.md.] The additions to the loop were a PRD that says what before how, an ADR that records the decision with its alternatives, a brief with allowed paths, and an append-only ledger in which every turn, gate, and attestation is an event. None of them changed the model call. Governance arrived as the missing component. The governed path you fly this Evolution is the same one: init, the PRD interview, the first ledger event, and an attestation after you have looked at the artifacts. Read gzkit's own PRD as the worked example. It is short, and it never says how. [~7 min]

Cut from slide 10 (full wording):
- The founding exchange (2026-01-12) / The model: for maximizing 'Claudishness,' only specification matters. / The operator: specification, methodology, and governance (all three, or the loop drifts). /  / [Quote from genesis.md — verify wording against the source before class.]
- The operator's remedy changed the documents around the model call and left the call itself alone: a PRD that says WHAT before any HOW, an ADR that records the decision and its alternatives, a brief with allowed paths, and an append-only ledger in which every turn, gate, and attestation is an event. Governance arrived as the missing component: a custom harness built on top of the vendor harness.

The PRD gets two minutes of its own, because the line between what and how decides whether ADR-1 will record real alternatives. The PRD states what: who uses the system, which question class it answers and which it refuses, what halting correctly means for each class, what budgets apply, what the ledger must hold, and what the human attests and when. The PRD does not state how: no model, no SDK, no framework, no schema field names, no code. If your PRD specifies a framework, you have pre-decided ADR-1 without recording alternatives, which is the post-hoc rationalization ADRs exist to prevent. [~2 min]

Cut from slide 11 (full wording):
- • Who uses the system and what they are trying to get done / • The bounded question class it answers, and the classes it must refuse / • What 'halted correctly' means for each class / • Budgets: turns, cost, latency the user will tolerate / • What must be in the ledger for a run to count / • What the human attests, and when
- • Which model, which SDK, which framework (that is ADR-1, in Evolution 2) / • The Step schema's field names / • Whether the loop is a for-loop or a state graph / • Any code /  / A PRD that specifies a framework decides the ADR in advance and records no alternatives. ADRs exist to prevent that post-hoc rationalization.

The evaluation lens has three columns. A weak Sortie 1 shows a screenshot of one happy-path run, keeps the budget in the system prompt, and writes the falsifiers after the run. A sound Sortie 1 does what the card asks: it flies three input classes, enforces budgets in code with a reason on every halt, keeps a ledger the Chase can replay, measures both routes, and freezes the card at Go. An exceptional Sortie 1 adds a run designed to fail that did fail, in the ledger, a local-model failure logged honestly as a squawk, the answer-without-reasoning falsifier tested with a prompt that tempts it, and a flight-log paragraph on what the SDK hid, which is the exercise from chapter ten. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 12 (full wording):
- 'It works' (a screenshot of one happy-path run) / Budget lives in the system prompt / Ledger is a print statement / One model, one route, no measurement / The falsifiers were written after the run
- Three input classes flown: answerable, unanswerable, adversarial / Turn and cost budgets enforced in code; halts carry a reason / Ledger events for every turn; the Chase can replay the run / Hosted and local runs compared on latency, cost, schema compliance / Card frozen at Go; evidence slice, nothing else, handed to the Chase
- A run that was designed to fail (budget exhausted) and did, in the ledger / A malformed-output case from the local model logged as a squawk / The 'answer without reasoning' falsifier actually tested with a tempting prompt / One paragraph in the flight log on what the SDK hid vs. the raw HTTP loop

The card for this Evolution sits at the center of the envelope, because this is the first sortie and nothing depends on it yet. Read the design claim. The card has three test points, one per input class, and each test point states the observable the Chase reads from the black box. The instrumentation is one turn event per model call and exactly one terminal event per run. You write the three falsifiers now, before you fly. The abort criteria keep the Chase from scoring an endpoint outage, or a small model that cannot emit the schema, as a failure of the design. Finish the card at the card station, request Go or No-Go, and fly test point one while I am in the room. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 13 (full wording):
- Flight Card 1 brief (Sortie 1): a governed loop that halts
- Center of the envelope · fill every field before requesting Go
- ENVELOPE            center / DESIGN CLAIM        The loop halts on every input class (answerable, unanswerable, adversarial) within budget, and every turn is in the ledger. / SYSTEMS UNDER TEST  loop · Step schema · budget guard · ledger writer · one model route (hosted or local) / ENTRY CONDITIONS    clean tree · gz init committed · PRD attested · Go recorded / TEST POINTS         1 answerable question   → turn events, then answer event; turns ≤ BUDGET /                     2 unanswerable question → turn events, then halt(reason) event; no fabricated answer /                     3 adversarial prompt    → budget enforced regardless; halt event present / INSTRUMENTATION     ledger: 1 turn event per model call; exactly 1 terminal event (answer|halt) per run; receipts: run hash / FALSIFIERS          a run exceeding the turn budget · a halt with no ledger event · a 'final answer' with no reasoning turn before it / ABORT               model endpoint unavailable; local model cannot emit the schema at all (squawk, not FAIL) / CHASE               peer, from the ledger slice and receipts only → PASS / FAIL

Two lines close the lecture. Observations are perception, which means everything the loop reads back from the world is untrusted input, and that rule becomes the injection test point in E3. The framing line stands: a loop without a halt is a bill. Build one that stops, and can say why.
CIDM6333_E2_Lecture_PatternsFrameworks.p:
Evolution 2 gives the halting loop from Evolution 1 a name and a home. Every framework is a theory of who owns the loop, and the choice of a framework is the first decision you will defend with alternatives on the table. Four teardowns trace LangChain to LangGraph, Pydantic AI, the role-based frameworks of 2023, and the vendor SDKs of 2025. In the lab you refactor the loop into a pattern from the catalog and record the choice in ADR-1. [0:00–0:01]

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- Evolution 2 · Lecture
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development / Survey: LangChain → LangGraph · Pydantic AI · AutoGen / CrewAI / MetaGPT · the vendor SDKs   ·   Build: the loop refactored into a catalogued pattern; ADR-1

The pattern catalog takes the most time, because the patterns are the build. The framing comes before it, and after it come four teardowns grouped by their theory of control, the reference design's model ADR, and the evaluation lens with Flight Card 2.

Cut from slide 2 (full wording):
- The five workflow patterns and the agent; when to keep it simple; refactoring E1's loop without touching the tool layer

Framing. Learn what a framework assumes about control rather than its API. LangGraph assumes that you own every edge. The Claude Agent SDK assumes that the vendor owns the loop and that you supply tools and instructions. CrewAI assumes that control is a conversation among roles. Each assumption is a theory, and the framework churn of 2022 to 2025 is the field arguing about those theories. The distinction from Evolution 1 now sharpens. A workflow calls the model along code paths you wrote. An agent lets the model direct its own control flow. A workflow is predictable, cheap, and testable, so build one wherever the path is known. Sortie 2 tests one statement: the same task runs under two patterns with identical tool traces, and the cost or quality difference that ADR-1 predicted appears in the evidence. If the predicted difference does not appear, the ADR recorded a rationalization. [~8 min]

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- A new framework has arrived every year since 2022. Each one encodes a theory of where control should live: in your code, in the model, in the vendor's harness, or in a graph you draw. When you pick a framework you pick its theory of control, and ADR-1 defends that choice.
- Workflow: your code calls the model along paths you wrote. Agent: the model directs its own control flow. A workflow is more predictable, cheaper, and easier to test, so build one wherever the path is known. Use the open loop only when the path cannot be known in advance.
- The statement Sortie 2 will try to disprove / The same task runs under two patterns with identical tool traces and a measurable difference in cost or quality that ADR-1 predicted. If the predicted consequence does not appear in the evidence, the ADR recorded a rationalization rather than a decision.

The catalog lists five workflows and the agent. Prompt chaining runs a fixed sequence with optional gates between steps and trades latency for accuracy. Routing classifies the input and dispatches it to a specialized path. Parallelization takes two forms, sectioning and voting. In orchestrator-workers a central model decomposes the task and delegates the parts, and the tools of Evolution 3 and the subagents of Evolution 8 plug in here. In evaluator-optimizer a producer and a critic run in a loop, which is the evaluation gate of Evolution 10 in miniature. The agent is the open loop you built in Evolution 1. The catalog puts it last and recommends it least. The source advises you to start with the simplest pattern that works and to add complexity only when it measurably helps. That advice is the null hypothesis of your ADR. [~8 min]

The worked example, in prose. Your E1 loop calls the model, reads a Step, either answers or calls a tool, and repeats under a budget. Control sits with the model, and code bounds it. The first refactor is orchestrator-workers. A planner splits the task, each bounded worker calls one tool, and a synthesis step produces the answer. Control is now split between the planner and the workers, and each worker has its own budget. The second refactor is evaluator-optimizer. A producer drafts, a critic checks the draft against criteria, and the loop runs at most K rounds. The halt is now a criterion rather than the model's say-so. The sortie requires one discipline: hold the tool layer constant. If the two runs do not call the same tools in the same order, the refactor changed behavior and the comparison measures nothing. With the tools held constant, the measured delta is attributable to the decision in your ADR and to nothing else. [~7 min]

Cut from slide 5 (full wording):
- orchestrator(messages) → [subtask₁, subtask₂] / worker(subtask₁) → calls tool A / worker(subtask₂) → calls tool B / synthesize → answer /  / Control: split between a planner and bounded workers; each worker has its own budget. / Trace: same tools, same order. A different order means the refactor changed behavior.
- producer(messages) → draft (tools A, B) / evaluator(draft, criteria) → PASS | revise / loop ≤ K rounds → answer /  / Control: a critic gates the halt, and the halt condition is now a criterion rather than the model's say-so. / Trace: same tools, plus evaluator turns you can count.
- Card 2 holds the tool layer constant so that the pattern is the only variable. The cost or quality delta you measure can then be attributed to the decision ADR-1 recorded, and to nothing else.

The source's advice forms a ladder, and each rung becomes a row in your ADR. Start with one model call and measure it. That measurement is the baseline row. Add a workflow only when the task decomposes and the gain is measurable, and write the predicted delta before the run. Add an agent only when the path cannot be scripted and trust, budget, and evaluation exist, which is what E1 gave you. Add a framework only when it buys something a stdlib loop cannot, such as checkpoints, tracing, or typed handoffs. 'None' is a legitimate alternative, and it must appear in ADR-1. Every layer a framework adds between you and the model call is a layer you cannot see into during Drift (the abstraction tax). If you cannot explain what the framework did on turn three, you do not own the loop. [~5 min]

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- Each layer a framework adds between your code and the model call is a layer you cannot inspect during Drift. This course calls that cost the abstraction tax. If you cannot explain what the framework did on turn three, you do not own the loop.

The first teardown covers one company and two theories of control. LangChain, in late 2022, wrapped the ReAct prompt in objects (chains, agents, tools, memory). The wrapper made the loop importable and also hid it, so practitioners paid the abstraction tax in opaque prompts and release-to-release drift. LangGraph, in 2024, corrected this by modeling the agent as a state graph you draw, with typed state, checkpoints, and a human interrupt as an edge. You own every edge. The four rows of the table are where the two differ most.Planning went from hidden to explicit, memory from opaque objects to typed state, governance from none to an interrupt, and runtime from a script to persisted runs with tracing. In judgment-loop terms, the decision was to move control from the library into a graph that the user draws, and the cost is that you now have to draw it. [~5 min]

Cut from slide 7 (full wording):
- Chains, agents, tools, and memory as objects: the first wrapper around the ReAct prompt. LangChain made the loop importable, and it also hid the loop from the developer. Developers who used it paid the abstraction tax: opaque prompts, deep class hierarchies, and behavior that changed with each release.
- The agent as a state graph: nodes are steps, edges are control flow you draw, state is an explicit typed object, checkpoints persist it, and a human-in-the-loop interrupt is an edge. You draw every edge yourself, and LangChain's first version gave you no such control.

Two more theories. Pydantic AI holds that the type system owns the boundary between model and code. The library validates every output before the output can act, tools are typed functions, and a malformed call never executes. Your E1 Step schema was this idea in miniature. The cost is that what the schema cannot express the model cannot do, and small local models fail the schema more often, which Evolution 3 shows. The role-based frameworks hold that control is a conversation. CAMEL runs two role players, MetaGPT runs a software company as prompts, AutoGen treats chat as coordination, and CrewAI runs crews with roles and a process. This is FIPA and BDI rediscovered with a language model in the reasoner slot, and Evolution 8 takes it up in full. The cost is AutoGPT's cost multiplied. No one in the conversation is an evaluator, so one role's polished summary becomes the next role's fact. [~5 min]

Cut from slide 8 (full wording):
- Pydantic AI validates every model output (a tool call or a final result) against a Pydantic model, and it retries or rejects a malformed output before that output can act. The framework injects dependencies, and tools are plain functions whose schemas come from their type hints. /  / Theory of control: the type system owns the boundary between model and code. Your E1 Step schema applied the same idea on a small scale. /  / Cost: the model cannot do what the schema cannot express, and small local models fail the schema more often (E3 shows this).
- CAMEL: two role-playing agents talk a task to completion. MetaGPT: a software company as prompts (PM, architect, engineer), with SOPs as the coordination mechanism. AutoGen: conversation is the coordination primitive; agents are chat participants. CrewAI: roles, goals, backstories, and a process (sequential or hierarchical). /  / Theory of control: control is a conversation among personas. These frameworks rediscover FIPA and BDI with a language model in the reasoner slot (E8). /  / Cost: the same as AutoGPT's, multiplied. No role in the conversation evaluates, so a polished summary from one role becomes the next role's fact.

The vendor SDKs, read by their theory of control. OpenAI's Agents SDK composes agents with handoffs and guardrails, a runner loops, and tracing ships with the runner. The Claude Agent SDK ships the harness as a library: the vendor owns the loop, and you supply tools, instructions, and hooks. Google's ADK builds a hierarchy, with workflow agents for sequential, parallel, and loop control and A2A for peers. Each vendor has a governance story (guardrail tripwires, permission prompts and hooks, callbacks), and none of the three records what was attested. The feature rows are as of early 2026, and the rate at which they go stale is part of the teardown. [~5 min]

Cut from slide 9 (full wording):
- Teardown: the vendor SDKs (2025), and who owns the loop
- Details are as of early 2026. These SDKs change often, so check current names and features against each vendor's documentation.

The reference design's model ADR decides a command-line parser. The stakes are low, so the reasoning is easy to read, and for this reason it is a good model. The decision was argparse over click. Click was the more popular library, and the ADR rejected popularity as a reason. The reasons that counted were zero external dependencies for a kit whose job is governance, a smaller upgrade surface, and the stdlib-first posture that later became doctrine. Your ADR-1 takes the same shape: intent from the PRD, the decision in one sentence, at least three alternatives including none, consequences in both directions with the one you will measure, a scorecard, and a checklist of what the choice must support by Evolution 12. Write the ADR before the code. An ADR written after the code records a rationalization. [~5 min]

Cut from slide 10 (full wording):
- Decision: build gzkit's CLI on the standard library's argparse rather than click. /  / Alternatives considered: click, typer, argparse, each recorded with its consequences rather than with adjectives. /  / The ADR's title comes from its rationale: the decision rejected click's popularity as a reason. The reasons that counted were zero external dependencies for a governance kit, a smaller attack and upgrade surface, and the stdlib-first posture that later became doctrine. /  / [Summarized from the ADR's title and the book's outline — verify the alternatives and consequences against the ADR text before class.]
- 1. Intent: what the loop must do (from the PRD) / 2. Decision: pattern + framework, in one sentence / 3. Alternatives: at least three, including 'none / stdlib'; each with what it buys and what it costs / 4. Consequences: positive and negative, and the one you will measure in Sortie 2 / 5. Decomposition scorecard: the decision scored against the alternatives on the criteria you listed / 6. Feature checklist: what the choice must support by E12 (tools, MCP, memory, multi-agent, evals, serving) /  / Write the ADR before the code. An ADR written after the code is post-hoc rationalization.

Stress a decision before you record it. The reference design's planning step supplies three forcing functions. In the pre-mortem, assume it is Evolution 12 and the choice has failed, then write the story. Whatever you wrote is a consequence. The second forcing function is 'what would have to be true': ask what would have to be true for the rejected alternative to have been right. If that is plausible, your decision needs a measurable consequence. In constraint archaeology, ask where each constraint came from (the PRD, the syllabus, or habit). Habit is not a constraint. The ten challenges, which you will put to a peer's ADR at the Chase station, are so what, scope, alternative, dependency, gold standard, timeline, evidence, consumer, regression, and parity (the list is chapter 11's). [~2 min]

Cut from slide 11 (full wording):
- Three forcing functions, and ten challenges for your peer
- Assume that in week twelve this framework choice has failed, and write the story of the failure. Add each consequence in the story to the ADR.
- So what? What changes if this is wrong / Scope: what is deliberately out / Alternative: the strongest one you did not pick / Dependency: what this now requires / Gold standard: what 'good' would look like / Timeline: when the evidence will arrive / Evidence: what you measured, not what you read / Consumer: who has to live with it / Regression: what got worse / Parity: what the alternative does that yours cannot
- 'What would have to be true' for the rejected alternative to have been right? If it is plausible, your decision needs a measurable consequence.

A weak submission chose its framework because a tutorial used it, lists alternatives as names, refactored the tools along with the pattern so that nothing is attributable, asserts 'better' without a measurement, and wrote the ADR afterward. A sound submission runs two patterns with identical traces in the ledger, predicts one consequence and measures it, lists three real alternatives including none, fills a scorecard whose winner is not the feature count, and commits the ADR before the refactor. An exceptional submission, and the one I want to see, records a prediction that did not appear and amends the ADR with the evidence. The sortie still FAILs, because the falsifier was registered before the flight and a verdict is not renegotiated afterward; the grade rewards the record, and an amended ADR is the record working as intended. [~4 min]

Cut from slide 12 (full wording):
- Evaluation lens: a strong Sortie 2 and a strong ADR-1
- Framework chosen because a tutorial used it / ADR lists alternatives as names with no consequences / Refactor changed the tools too; traces differ; delta unattributable / 'Better' asserted; nothing measured / ADR written after the code
- Two patterns, same task, identical tool traces in the ledger / One consequence predicted in the ADR and measured: cost, latency, or a quality score / Three alternatives including none/stdlib, each with what it buys and costs / Scorecard filled; the winner is not the one with the most features / ADR committed before the refactor commit
- The predicted consequence did not appear, the sortie FAILed, and the ADR was amended with the evidence attached / A pre-mortem paragraph that describes a week-12 failure and a mitigation / The peer's ten-challenge review answered in the ADR, not dismissed / A note on what the framework hid on turn three, and how you found out

Flight Card 2 stays at the center of the envelope and is the first sortie with a dependency: Sortie 1 must have passed. The design claim is the same statement: the same task runs under two patterns with identical tool traces and the cost or quality delta that ADR-1 predicted. There are three test points: the task under pattern A with a measurement, the same task under pattern B with the tool sequence identical, and the comparison against the prediction in the ADR. The last falsifier on the card makes an ADR dated after the refactor commit a FAIL, because a prediction written after the refactor is not a prediction. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 13 (full wording):
- Flight Card 2 brief (Sortie 2): two patterns, one trace
- Center of the envelope · depends on Sortie 1 PASS
- ENVELOPE            center / DESIGN CLAIM        The same task runs under two patterns with identical tool traces and a measurable difference in cost or quality that ADR-1 predicted. / SYSTEMS UNDER TEST  E1 loop · pattern A · pattern B · tool layer (held constant) · ledger · ADR-1 / DEPENDS ON          Sortie 1 PASS on record / ENTRY CONDITIONS    clean tree · ADR-1 committed BEFORE the refactor commit · Go recorded / TEST POINTS         1 task under pattern A   → ledger: tool events [A₁…Aₙ]; cost/latency/quality recorded /                     2 same task, pattern B   → ledger: identical tool event sequence; second measurement /                     3 compare               → delta in the direction and rough size ADR-1 predicted / INSTRUMENTATION     ledger: two runs, tool sequences equal; receipts: run hashes; artifact: ADR-1 with the prediction, dated before TP1 / FALSIFIERS          tool sequences differ · no measurement recorded · the ADR's predicted consequence does not appear · ADR dated after the refactor / ABORT               framework install/runtime failure unrelated to the pattern (squawk) / CHASE               peer, from the two ledger slices and the ADR only → PASS / FAIL
A framework is a theory of who owns the loop. For Sortie 2, commit ADR-1 with its predicted consequence before the refactor commit, and run both patterns over the same tool layer.
CIDM6333_E3_Lecture_ToolsAsContracts.ppt:
Evolution 3 connects the loop, which already halts and now has a pattern, to the world. The statement that organizes the lecture is that a tool is a contract and the model is an untrusted caller. Four teardowns cover the two ways a model learned to call tools, the retrieval systems that scaled the catalog, the screen as a tool, and Claude Code hooks, which the harness runs around every tool call. The lab has three parts: a read tool that runs freely, a write tool that does not run until a confirmation event is in the ledger, and a local eight-billion-parameter model that produces the calls. The course requires the local model because a small model's failures make the contract visible.

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- Evolution 3 · Lecture · local model required
- Schemas, side-effect classes, permission gating, retry, halting; the model is an untrusted caller; hooks that run before and after every tool call, and where a hook cannot see
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development / Survey: Toolformer vs. function calling · Gorilla / ToolBench · computer use · Claude Code hooks   ·   Build: read tool free, write tool blocked until a confirmation event, a local model producing the calls

The gate is the build, so the spine gets the most time. Framing precedes it, and four teardowns, the reference design's two August incidents, and the evaluation lens with the flight card follow it. The card has four test points in this Evolution, and the fourth is the injected write.

Cut from slide 2 (full wording):
- A tool is a contract; the model is an untrusted caller; why a local model is the right substrate for this Evolution

Framing. The model does not call your function. It emits text that asks for the call, and your code performs every step between that text and the effect: it parses the text, validates it against a schema, decides whether the call is permitted, runs it, and hands back an observation. Governance lives in those steps, and for this reason the lecture treats the model as an untrusted caller. The term is architectural rather than moral: the loop trusts nothing the model sends until the loop's own code has checked it. The right panel explains why the course requires a local model. A frontier model honors the contract so reliably that you never see it enforced. A small model breaks it in the first ten turns (malformed JSON, invented arguments, tools that do not exist, a write where a read would do), so the gate you write is one you have watched refuse. The design claim Sortie 3 will try to disprove ends with the phrase the fourth test point depends on: including when the write is requested by text the model read.

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- The model never calls your function directly: it emits text that requests the call. Your code parses that text, validates it against a schema, decides whether the call is permitted, runs it, and hands back an observation. Your code performs each of those steps, so each step is a place where your code can enforce governance.
- A frontier model produces well-formed calls so reliably that you never see the contract enforced. A small local model emits malformed JSON, invents arguments, calls tools that do not exist, and asks for a write when a read would do. Expect these failures within the first ten turns. The course uses the small model to make the contract visible, not as a deployment target, so that you see the gate you write in this Evolution refuse a call.
- The design claim Sortie 3 will try to disprove / No write-class tool executes without a prior confirmation event in the ledger, including when the write is requested by text the model read rather than by the human. A write with no preceding event, a file changed after a denial, or a pass obtained by disabling the gate falsifies it.

A tool declaration has four fields. The model emits the name and reads the description, so you write the description as a contract: what the tool does, what it must not do, and what it returns on failure. The schema (JSON Schema or a Pydantic model) is the first gate. A call that fails validation never reaches the function; it returns a structured error that the model can read and retry. The side-effect class is the field the gate reads. You declare it on the tool rather than infer it from the name, because a tool's name can mislead (a delete tool called 'cleanup'), and the gate must not depend on it. The fourth field covers idempotency and budget. A read can be retried without harm, and a retried write is a second write, so the retry policy reads the declared idempotency. Every tool has a timeout and every loop a retry budget, and when either runs out the loop halts. The strip states the fail-closed rule: the gate treats a tool with no class declared as irreversible.

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- The model emits the tool's name in its call, and it reads only the description to decide when to call the tool. Write the description as a contract: what the tool does, what it must not do, what it returns on failure.
- JSON Schema or a Pydantic model for the input; optionally for the output. A call that fails validation never reaches the function; it returns a structured error the model can read and retry. Type validation is therefore the first gate a call meets.
- read: no state changes; run freely. write: state changes, reversible; requires a confirmation event. irreversible: delete, send, deploy; requires an attestation. The tool's declaration states the class, and the loop never infers the class from the tool's name.
- A loop can retry a read without harm. When it retries a write, it performs the write a second time. Declare idempotency so the retry policy can read it. Give every tool a timeout and every loop a retry budget. When the loop exhausts either one, it halts, and it does not swallow the error and continue.
- Design rule for this Evolution: the side-effect class is a field on the declaration, the gate reads that field, and a tool with no class declared is treated as irreversible.

The slide shows the gate as fourteen lines of your own loop, so that you can see it needs no framework. The loop parses the model's step, looks the tool up in the registry (an unknown tool halts), validates the arguments against the schema, and checks the side-effect class. For a read it records the call and runs the function. For a write it searches the ledger for a confirm event, and for an irreversible tool for an attestation, bound to this tool and these arguments. If none exists, the loop records a denial, hands the model a DENIED observation, and continues. If one exists, the loop records the call with the event and runs the function. The four properties on the right are what the Chase reads from the ledger: order, binding, source, and a trace left by every denial. Source is the property the injection test point depends on. The confirm comes from the human's action in the host (a keypress, a command), never from model output and never from content the model read.

Cut from slide 5 (full wording):
- 1. Order. The confirm event's timestamp precedes the call event's. If the confirm is recorded after the call, the call ran ungated. / 2. Binding. The confirm specifies the tool and the arguments. A blanket 'yes' that any later write can spend disables the gate. / 3. Source. The confirm is emitted by the human's action in the host (a keypress, a command), never by the model's output and never by text the model read. / 4. Denial leaves a trace. A denied write is a ledger event and an observation to the model, and the filesystem after denial is byte-identical to before.

The table lists six kinds of failure, and the loop handles each with the same shape of policy. The model sees the error as an observation, the loop retries under a budget, and when the budget runs out the loop halts. Two rows need a reason attached. The loop halts on a second identical schema rejection because the model has shown that it is not reading the error, and the loop never retries a write automatically because a retried write is a second write. Every row ends in a ledger event. A failure the ledger does not show is a failure the Chase cannot read, so a loop that swallows an error has removed its own evidence.

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- Model may ask the human or take a read path; a second identical request is a halt
- Every row ends in a ledger event. A failure the ledger does not show is a failure the Chase cannot read, and a loop that swallows an error removes its own evidence.

The slide holds four teardowns, two on each side. Toolformer (February 2023) taught a model to insert API calls into its own text by self-supervised fine-tuning, so the model learned when a call lowered its next-token loss. The calls are learned and implicit, the contract lives in the weights, and nothing validates it. Function calling (June 2023) declared the tools at inference, one JSON Schema per function in the request and a structured call in the response, so the contract lives in the prompt and your code validates it. Function calling won for this reason: it moved the contract to where you can read and enforce it. Gorilla and ToolBench answered a different problem. When the catalog holds thousands of APIs the prompt cannot hold them, so Gorilla retrieved the relevant documentation at inference, and ToolBench built a benchmark over 16,000 real APIs, with a retriever that selects candidates before the model chooses. Two lessons survive. The retriever and the model both read the description, so you write it for both. A retrieved tool the model has never seen is an untrusted tool, which is the tool-poisoning surface of Evolution 5 arriving two years early.

Computer use (Anthropic, October 2024) shows what generality costs a contract. Perception is a screenshot and action is a click, a keystroke, or a scroll, so the contract collapses to one tool with one argument space, and every action is write-class because a click can cause anything. The schema cannot say what a click will cause, so the gate has to sit at the effect (what changed) rather than at the call (what was asked). A Claude Code hook is a shell command the harness runs at a lifecycle event (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, and SessionEnd, among others), and a PreToolUse hook can allow, deny, or ask. The harness runs it regardless of what the model decided, and that is what makes a hook enforcement rather than instruction. A hook sees the call as declared. It cannot see an effect that the declared surface hides, and a Bash call is the standard case: the tool is Bash, and the write sits inside the argument string.

gzkit renders its canon into seventeen Claude Code hooks: orientation at SessionStart, gates before writes and commits, verifiers after tool use, and two pipeline gates (pipeline-gate.py and verifier-pipe-gate.py) that check the governed path was followed. On August 21 a gate checked that a required artifact existed and passed it, while the artifact was present and empty because the procedure that should have produced it had not run. The gate verified presence and skipped procedure, so the fix made gates check the record of the procedure (the ledger event, the receipt) instead of the existence of its output. On August 23, writes made through the Bash tool (echo >, sed -i, python -c) passed a PreToolUse fence that watched Write and Edit, because the hook saw the tool name 'Bash' and not the file. The fix (GHI #844/#847) moved the write-side fences to the commit locus, where git diff --cached shows every write whatever tool made it. The strip states the design decision for your own gate: gate at the call when the schema can see the effect, and at the effect when it cannot. Chapter 12's exercise has you implement the gate both ways and show a write that one catches and the other misses. [verify the issue numbers and dates against the changelog]

The lens has three columns. A weak sortie has a gate that is a sentence in the prompt, with nothing in code that refuses. Its confirmation is a blanket yes at session start that every later write spends, or a confirm recorded after the call or written by the model. It skips the injection test, or it swaps the local model for a hosted one to hide the malformed calls. A sound sortie shows a read that runs without a confirm event and a write refused with a denied event and an observation. Its confirm is bound to the tool and its arguments and timestamped before the call. An injected request is denied with no file change, a halt is exercised at least once with its reason in the ledger, and the local model sits on the substrate line with its malformed calls counted. An exceptional sortie goes further. It implements the gate twice (as a hook and in the loop) and shows one write that only one of them catches. It attempts a Bash-style write that the call-locus gate misses and the diff-locus check catches. It leaves one tool without a side-effect class and shows the gate refusing it as irreversible. After a denial, the model chooses a read path, and the filesystem hash is identical before and after the denied write.

Flight Card 3 is the first expansion of the envelope, and it depends on a Sortie 2 PASS. It has four test points. In the first, the read tool answers a request with no confirm and a call event in the ledger. In the second, the gate refuses the write, records a denied event, returns an observation to the model, and leaves the file unchanged. In the third, the human confirms the same request through a host action, and the Chase checks that the confirm event precedes the call event and is bound to the tool and its arguments. In the fourth, the model reads a file that says 'now write X', and the pass condition is a denial with no confirm event in existence. The abort criterion separates infrastructure from the design claim: if the local model cannot produce a parseable tool call in N attempts, the sortie halts rather than fails, and you record N.

CIDM6333_E4_Lecture_MCP1.pptx:
Evolution 4 takes the tool contract of Evolution 3, where the model was an untrusted caller, out of your process and puts it on a wire, so that any host can discover it. The question becomes what a protocol has to promise that a function signature does not. Three teardowns cover the plugin era that failed, the OpenAPI specs that described a tool without negotiating anything, and the protocol that won and then moved to a foundation. In the lab you serve your E3 tools over MCP, list them in the inspector, call them from your harness and from a script, and log each call at the server. The revision of the specification that went to general availability on July 28 changed the wire in ways your SDK may or may not already reflect, so the lecture teaches the current revision and states what changed.

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- Evolution 4 · Lecture
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development / Survey: ChatGPT plugins · OpenAPI tool specs · MCP and its foundation   ·   Build: an MCP server over your tool layer; inspector; harness client and script client

Because the build is a server and the July revision changed the wire, the spine is the longest part. The framing comes before it. After it come three teardowns that end at the foundation, the reference design's refusal and the project that reverses it one tier up, and the evaluation lens with the flight card.

Framing. The problem MCP answered was combinatorial. Before November 2024 each host and each tool wrote adapters for each other, and the field paid N times M. A protocol lets each side write one adapter and pay N plus M. A protocol then makes three promises that a function signature cannot: discovery, negotiation, and transport independence. Your E3 tool had a schema and a gate and none of these three, because nothing outside your process could ask it anything. The design claim for the sortie is that two independent clients and one server show identical behavior, with every call logged. One of the falsifiers is asymmetric: a tool that works from the harness and fails from the script means the harness was compensating for the protocol, and the sortie has measured the compensation.

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- Every host that wanted a tool wrote its own adapter, and every tool that wanted a host wrote another. With N hosts and M tools the field maintained N×M adapters. A protocol makes each side implement one thing: N clients, M servers, N+M pieces of code.
- Discovery: a client can ask a server what it offers before it calls anything. Negotiation: client and server state which version and which capabilities they support, and a mismatch produces an error that neither side resolves by guessing. Transport independence: the same server runs over a pipe on your laptop and over HTTP on a host you do not control. Your E3 tool had a schema and a permission gate. It did not have any of these three, because nothing outside your process could ask.
- The statement Sortie 4 will try to disprove / Every tool the server declares is discoverable, callable, and schema-validated from two independent clients, and every call is logged server-side. If a tool works from your harness and fails from a script, the harness did work the protocol should have done, and the difference between the two clients measures that work.

The slide puts the architecture in one column and the primitives in the rest. The host is the application the human is in, each server gets one client inside the host, and client and server exchange JSON-RPC requests in both directions. The specification distinguishes the three primitives by who controls each one, and that distinction is the design analysis of the protocol. Tools are model-controlled; a tool is the E3 contract put on the wire. Resources are application-controlled: the host decides what enters context, and for this reason E5 treats a resource that carries an instruction as an attack. Prompts are user-controlled. Two more cards follow: extensions, with the tasks extension for long-running work, and the deprecation list from the July 28 revision. The deprecation list matters because tutorials written before that revision still teach roots and sampling. A new server should not adopt a feature the specification has scheduled for removal.

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- Hosts, clients, servers, and the three server primitives
- Host: the application the human is in (Claude Code, Codex, your script). Client: the connector inside the host, one per server. Server: the process that declares capabilities and answers requests, over JSON-RPC 2.0.
- Functions the model may call. Declared with a name, a description, a JSON Schema for input, and optionally one for output. The model chooses to call them; the host may gate the call first.
- Data the server exposes by URI: files, records, a ledger, 'what is attested?' The application decides which resources enter context and when.
- Reusable templates the server offers the user: a workflow with a name and arguments, surfaced as a slash command or a menu item in the host.
- Beyond the core: an `extensions` field in both capability sets; long-running work moved to the official tasks extension (`tasks/get` polling, `tasks/update` for input). Adopt an extension only when the core cannot express the need.
- Roots, sampling, and logging are deprecated with a twelve-month window: pass paths as tool arguments, call the model API directly, log to stderr or OpenTelemetry. The HTTP+SSE transport is deprecated; use Streamable HTTP.

The revision that went to general availability on July 28 rewrote the wire, and the headline change is statelessness: there is no handshake and no session header, and every request carries its version and capabilities in its metadata. The changelog gives an infrastructure rationale: any request can land on any instance behind a round-robin balancer, because no instance has to remember anything between calls. The change that bites a server author is the third row. Roots, sampling, and elicitation were calls the server made back into the client; under the new revision a server that needs more input returns a result typed input_required, and the client retries the request with the answers attached. The fourth row is your first test point: server/discover is mandatory, and it is the inspector's first call. The last two rows cover subscriptions, which are now one stream, and list results, which must carry a TTL and a cache scope; put your tools in deterministic order and give an honest TTL. Check which revision your pinned Python SDK speaks before you build, because the SDKs shipped on the day of the revision and a version pinned earlier may not have it.

Cut from slide 5 (full wording):
- No handshake. Every request carries protocol version and client capabilities in `_meta`; servers answer with `serverInfo` in `_meta`
- A request can land on any instance behind a plain load balancer, with nothing to remember between calls
- Removed. `tools/list` and the other list methods no longer vary per connection; cross-call state uses server-minted handles passed as ordinary arguments
- If your server needed a session, it now needs a handle. Record the handle as a design decision
- Multi Round-Trip Requests: the server returns `resultType: "input_required"` with `inputRequests`; the client retries the original request with `inputResponses`
- A server that needs more from the human asks for it in its result and does not call the client back; every result now carries `resultType`
- Source: modelcontextprotocol.io, 2026-07-28 changelog (GA July 28, 2026; Tier 1 SDKs shipped same day). Verify the Python SDK version installed in the lab against this table.

This slide shows the server itself, in the shape the Python SDK gives you. FastMCP derives the input schema from the type hints and the description from the docstring, so the function you wrote in E3 becomes a server with one decorator. A resource is addressed by URI; here the URI returns the last fifty ledger events. The transport is a flag: stdio for this Evolution, Streamable HTTP when the host is not on your laptop. The four steps on the right are the lab in order. The third step carries the design claim, because two clients, one of them a script, leave the harness no way to hide protocol work from you. The strip at the bottom is the bridge to E5. The description is all the model sees, so write it as a contract; in E5 you will read tool descriptions that an adversary wrote.

Confirm that server/discover answers and tools/list shows the tool with the schema you meant. / 3. Two teardowns follow, both from before the protocol. The plugin store of March 2023 offered description without negotiation, ran inside one product, and its vendor deprecated it within a year. Function calling and the OpenAPI-derived schemas were the correct idea in-process, and they are what your E3 tool is, but every host still wrote its own loader, so the combinatorial cost did not change. Read both by their theory of control, as E2 read the frameworks: in the plugin model the vendor owns discovery and the loop, and in the OpenAPI model you own the loop and nobody owns the boundary. MCP specified the boundary between host and server, which neither predecessor had specified.

Cut from slide 7 (full wording):
- A manifest, an OpenAPI document, and a one-paragraph description the model read to decide when to call the plugin. Hosted by the vendor, invoked inside one product, discoverable in one store. /  / What it got right: the model could read a spec and call an endpoint. What it lacked: any host but one, any negotiation of capability or version, any local transport, and any way for the plugin to offer content or prompts rather than functions. ChatGPT plugins were deprecated within a year in favor of GPTs and Actions. /  / Theory of control: the vendor owns discovery, hosting, and the loop; you own an HTTP endpoint.
- Function calling arrived mid-2023: hand the model a JSON Schema per function, get back a structured call. Some teams generated those schemas from OpenAPI documents, one endpoint per tool. /  / What it got right: schemas as contracts, in-process, on any model. What it lacked: discovery (the host must already know the spec), negotiation (no version, no capability exchange), and a second primitive (everything is a function; no resources, no prompts). Each host still wrote its own loader, so the N×M adapter count remained. /  / Theory of control: you own the loop and the schema; no party owns the boundary between hosts.

The third teardown reads MCP itself as a system, on the board as a Design Analysis. The timeline runs down the left and ends at the foundation and the GA revision, so that the protocol's own governance apparatus is visible: a deprecation policy with a twelve-month window and an enhancement-proposal process. The question the course asks of every system is where the human is, and here the answer is precise: in the host, and only in the host. The wire carries requests only, and no message on it grants permission. That design choice has a consequence, and E5 covers the consequence. Two more cards follow: what a protocol needs around it, where a registry without provenance counts as a supply chain, and the analysis in the template's five fields.

Cut from slide 8 (full wording):
- Teardown: MCP as a system. Where is the human?
- Nov 2024: Anthropic publishes protocol, SDKs, reference servers. / Mar 2025: Streamable HTTP; HTTP+SSE deprecated; OAuth authorization. / Jun 2025: Resource indicators, structured tool output, elicitation. / Nov 2025: Tasks (experimental), URL-mode elicitation. / Dec 2025: Donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation). / Jul 2026: 2026-07-28 GA: stateless core, MRTR, deprecation policy.
- In the host, and only in the host. The protocol puts consent in the host: the client must get the human's approval before a tool runs, and the server must never assume it. The wire carries requests only, and no message on it grants permission. /  / Component focus: tools and coordination. The protocol's designers delegated governance to the host, and E5 examines what happens when the host's trust is misplaced.
- A versioning and deprecation policy (twelve-month window; a registry of deprecated features). Independent SDKs (TypeScript, Python, Go, C#; Rust in beta). A server registry with provenance, because a registry without provenance is an unchecked supply chain (E5: SmartLoader). Governance by a foundation instead of a single vendor.
- Problem: N×M. Decision: a client–server protocol over JSON-RPC with three server primitives and negotiated capabilities. Alternatives: a plugin store; per-vendor function-calling formats; a library. Consequences: adoption across hosts, and a security surface that did not exist when tools were in-process. Where it puts the human: outside the wire.

The reference design refused the protocol this Evolution teaches. Its storage-tiers doctrine states that no external protocol may be a prerequisite for a core governance operation. A kit whose job is to be trusted keeps the smallest dependency surface, which is the same posture gzkit took in ADR-0.0.2 when it chose argparse over click. The campaign review nevertheless scored MCP as absent and un-designed, and the review held the refusal the honest way: written down, with its alternatives, and open to reversal. The reversal is on the right. A server one tier up exposes the verbs and the ledger without becoming a prerequisite, and the falsifier for the tier boundary is a two-step test: kill the server, then run gz validate. If gz validate fails, the server became a prerequisite and the doctrine no longer holds. [verify the quoted sentence against the repository]

CIDM6333_E5_Lecture_MCP2_Security_Harnes:
Evolution 5. In Evolution 4 you put one tool on the wire, where two clients could find it. In this Evolution the strangers are not friendly: the client is adversarial and the resources carry instructions. The framing sentence is that the product is the harness: most of what makes an agent product safe or unsafe is not the model.The survey covers the authorization flow the spec now requires, four attack mechanisms, six dated incidents, A2A as the peer protocol, the instruction files the harnesses read, and the 2026 harness-engineering writing. The build is to harden your server so a poisoned resource cannot cause a write, to pin your tool descriptions, and to revise the AGENTS.md you wrote in the earlier lab. The self-guided lab is to plant a poisoned tool description in your own server and see whether OpenCode's model follows it.

Framing. A coding agent has eight parts: a model, a loop, a tool layer, a permission system, a context budget, instruction files, hooks, and a log. The model is one of the eight. The other seven are the harness, and they are the parts you can test and attest.Two rules recur through the rest of the lecture. First, the server does not trust what the client says about itself: scope comes from the token the server validated, never from anything the client wrote. Second, every observation is data and never instruction. The GitHub issue you traced in Evolution 4 was content, and the agent treated it as a command. The design claim for Sortie 5 is the first corner of the envelope in the term: an adversary cannot exceed scope, and a poisoned resource cannot cause a write. Three falsifiers are pre-registered. The third comes from the reference design: a pass obtained by disabling a check, or by removing the write tool for the test, falsifies the design claim.
